title: You are not using AI wrong. Your AI is just in the wrong place.
abstract: The real friction isn’t the writing—it’s the tab switching, copying, pasting, lost heading structure, and manual re-indenting that comes after. CasperWasp Document Studio puts the AI panel inside the editor, so your content lands where you’re already working—formatted, contextual, and ready to use. Less fixing. More creating. AI, right where your document lives.

title: Information-Theoretic Analysis of Neural Network Training Dynamics
abstract: This paper presents a novel information-theoretic analysis of neural network training dynamics. Traditional approaches to understanding neural network training often rely on simplified gradient-based methods and empirical observations, lacking a rigorous theoretical foundation. We argue that a more insightful perspective can be gained by framing neural network training as an information processing task. We leverage concepts from information theory, specifically mutual information and entropy, to characterize the flow of information during the training process. Our analysis provides a framework for quantifying the reduction of uncertainty about the optimal parameters, which directly relates to convergence rates and generalization performance. We demonstrate how the rate of information gain, measured through mutual information, can be linked to the learning dynamics. Furthermore, we explore the impact of regularization terms on the entropy of the parameter space, offering a new lens for understanding their role in promoting generalization. The core contribution of this work is a formal information-theoretic framework for analyzing neural network training, offering a more nuanced and potentially more predictive understanding of this complex process.

title: Hierarchical Bayesian Networks for Forecasting Complex Time Series
abstract: This paper investigates the application of Hierarchical Bayesian Networks (HBNs) for forecasting complex time series data. Traditional Bayesian networks often fail to adequately represent the intricate hierarchical dependencies prevalent in real-world time series, leading to suboptimal forecasting performance. This work proposes a novel HBN architecture designed to explicitly model these dependencies at multiple levels of abstraction. The core mechanism involves constructing a network where higher-level nodes represent aggregated trends, while lower-level nodes capture finer-grained fluctuations. This approach allows for a more nuanced and accurate representation of the underlying dynamics, ultimately improving forecasting robustness. We present a mathematical framework for the HBN, detailing the probabilistic models and inference algorithms employed. The paper focuses on the theoretical underpinnings and architectural design of the HBN, providing a foundation for future research and practical implementation. The key contribution is a systematic method for building hierarchical models that can effectively handle the complexities of time series forecasting.

title: Causal Inference with Dynamic Bayesian Networks and Granger Causality Tests
abstract: Traditional Bayesian networks offer a powerful framework for representing and reasoning about causal relationships. However, they often struggle to accurately represent systems where causal connections are not static but evolve over time. This paper introduces a novel approach that combines dynamic Bayesian networks (DBNs) with Granger causality tests to address this limitation. The proposed framework allows for the identification and adaptation of causal relationships within a system as new data becomes available. The core innovation lies in using Granger causality tests – a statistical method for determining if one time series predicts another – as a mechanism for updating the structure of the dynamic Bayesian network. This process generates a more robust and accurate representation of evolving causal dynamics. The methodology is presented with a clear theoretical foundation and demonstrates the potential for improved causal inference in complex, time-varying systems. The system is modeled using DBNs and Granger causality tests to identify and update causal relationships over time, allowing for the modeling of evolving causal structures in complex systems.

title: Cognitive Architecture Based on Time Flow: Semantic Representation
abstract: This paper proposes a novel cognitive architecture grounded in the concept of "time flow," aiming to enhance cognitive understanding and reasoning by explicitly incorporating temporal information. Traditional cognitive architectures often treat knowledge and experience as static representations, neglecting the crucial role of time in shaping human cognition. This architecture addresses this limitation by representing knowledge and experience as sequences of events along a time flow. We leverage time series analysis techniques to perform knowledge reasoning based on these temporal sequences and utilize the temporal relationships between events to establish semantic associations. The core claim of this work is that constructing a time-flow based cognitive architecture, utilizing time-ordering information for richer semantic representation, will improve cognitive tasks' understanding and reasoning capabilities. The proposed mechanism focuses on transforming knowledge and experience into temporal event sequences, applying time series analysis for knowledge inference, and exploiting event temporal relationships for semantic connections. We believe this approach offers a more biologically plausible and effective model of human cognition. ---

title: Context-Aware Relational Reasoning via Bayesian Networks with Temporal Dependencies
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to relational reasoning by integrating Bayesian Networks with temporal dependencies and contextual influences. Traditional Bayesian Networks struggle to represent the dynamic and context-dependent nature of relationships observed in many real-world scenarios. Our method extends Bayesian Network inference to explicitly model time-varying probabilities and incorporate contextual factors, enabling dynamic updates and significantly improved relational predictions. We introduce a framework where the strength of relationships is not fixed but evolves over time, influenced by surrounding circumstances. This approach addresses the inherent limitations of static Bayesian Networks and provides a more robust and accurate representation of complex relational dynamics. The core of the method lies in defining temporal Bayesian Networks (TBNs), which allows us to represent how relationships change over time and how these changes are affected by the context. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through conceptual formulations, highlighting its advantages and outlining future research directions.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Based Distributed Algorithm Verification Framework
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for distributed algorithm verification leveraging quantum entanglement. The core claim centers on the ability to independently verify algorithms without relying on shared keys or classical communication, thereby enhancing both verification efficiency and security. The proposed mechanism utilizes a set of entangled particles, each representing a component of the algorithm, enabling direct assessment of correctness through measurements of the entangled state. This approach circumvents the limitations of traditional distributed verification methods regarding security and efficiency. The framework offers a fundamentally new approach to algorithm verification, capitalizing on the core principles of quantum mechanics. The overall goal is to establish a robust and efficient method for validating distributed quantum algorithms. This document details the framework's architecture, key components, and theoretical underpinnings, focusing on the core principles and potential applications. ---

title: Topological Quantum Bit-Based Quantum Key Distribution Protocol
abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol leveraging the unique properties of topological quantum bits (TQBs). Traditional QKD protocols are vulnerable to attacks exploiting imperfections in quantum hardware. TQBs, due to their inherent robustness against local perturbations and decoherence, offer a promising solution for enhancing security. This protocol, termed TQB-QKD, utilizes the topological protection inherent in TQBs to establish a key between two parties, Alice and Bob. The core of the protocol revolves around the measurement of the non-local properties of TQBs, resulting in a highly secure key exchange. We detail the protocol's key generation steps, error correction, and privacy amplification stages, emphasizing the advantages derived from TQB characteristics. The protocol is designed to mitigate potential attacks targeting qubit decoherence and measurement errors, offering a pathway towards more secure and practical QKD systems. The theoretical analysis demonstrates the improved security margin compared to conventional QKD protocols.

title: Decentralized Federated Learning with Differential Privacy using Threshold Cryptography
abstract: Federated learning (FL) presents a promising approach to training machine learning models on decentralized data sources while preserving user privacy. However, traditional FL methods often rely on a central server, introducing a single point of failure and potential privacy risks. This paper proposes a novel decentralized federated learning system that leverages threshold cryptography and differential privacy to address these concerns. The core claim is that protecting user privacy in federated learning remains a significant challenge, and this system provides a robust solution. The system operates through a series of distributed rounds where participants collaboratively update model parameters using threshold cryptography to ensure secure aggregation and differential privacy to mitigate individual data exposure. This approach eliminates the need for a central server, enhancing both privacy and security. The system is designed for scalability and adaptability, making it suitable for various decentralized data scenarios. This work contributes to the development of more secure and privacy-preserving federated learning solutions.

title: Title: Topological Information Theory – Quantum Geometry and Computation
abstract: This paper explores the intersection of topology, geometry, and computation, proposing a novel computational paradigm based on quantum geometry. We investigate how quantum topology, specifically through quantum geometry, can be leveraged to achieve precise quantum simulation and algorithm validation. The core mechanism involves encoding quantum states using topological structures and utilizing quantum effects for optimization and verification. The work addresses a gap in current computational methods by offering a fundamentally different approach to quantum information processing, potentially offering increased precision and efficiency compared to traditional methods. This research lays the groundwork for a new era in quantum computation, leveraging the principles of topology to create robust and adaptable quantum algorithms.

title: Quantum State Dynamic Parameter Adjustment and Topological Structure Optimization
abstract: Quantum state dynamics are a fundamental aspect of quantum computation, and their manipulation offers a powerful route to accelerating quantum algorithms and enhancing their efficiency. This paper investigates a novel approach to quantum state dynamics, employing dynamic parameter adjustments and topological structure optimization. We propose a framework that leverages the inherent properties of quantum states to dynamically optimize key parameters, thereby minimizing errors and increasing computational throughput. The core mechanism focuses on strategically modifying the state's evolution through a combination of parameter adjustments and topology-driven transformations. This approach aims to surpass the limitations of conventional methods, offering a more robust and efficient path toward advancing quantum technology. The results demonstrate a significant improvement in algorithm performance compared to existing approaches, highlighting the potential of this dynamic system.

title: 基于高斯分布的复杂模型参数优化
abstract: This paper presents a novel algorithm for complex model parameter optimization utilizing the Gaussian distribution as a core optimization strategy. Traditional optimization methods often rely on fixed parameters, while this approach dynamically adjusts parameters to improve model prediction accuracy. The proposed algorithm employs the Gaussian distribution to systematically explore the parameter space, leading to enhanced model performance. We analyze the algorithm's effectiveness through simulations and demonstrate its superior performance compared to existing methods in a range of model types. The core mechanism centers around the utilization of Gaussian distributions to guide parameter adjustments, resulting in more precise predictions. This research offers a significant advancement in parameter optimization techniques applicable to a variety of complex modeling tasks.

title: Adaptive Geometry Model Optimization for Self-Adaptive Machine Learning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel self-adaptive machine learning framework for the optimization of non-linear geometry models. Traditional machine learning methods often struggle with the inherent complexities of non-linear geometric models, resulting in instability and inefficiency. Our proposed framework dynamically adjusts the parameters of the geometry model to enhance the stability and efficiency of the learning process. This adaptation occurs in real-time, allowing the model to continuously refine its representation of the underlying geometric structure. The core mechanism centers around a feedback loop that leverages gradient-based optimization, coupled with a novel parameter adjustment strategy inspired by biological neural networks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of illustrative examples, showcasing improvements in both model stability and learning speed compared to baseline methods. The framework offers a promising path towards more robust and efficient machine learning for complex geometric modeling problems.

title: Anti-Forgetting Adaptive Teacher-Driven Knowledge Distillation for Medical Image Classification
abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success in medical image classification, yet their performance remains sensitive to dataset size. Knowledge distillation (KD) alleviates this issue by transferring knowledge from a high-capacity teacher to a lightweight student. However, conventional KD relies on a static teacher, while adaptive teacher updating may improve performance on the student-learning data while reducing retention of knowledge acquired during teacher pretraining. To address these limitations, we propose an Anti-forgetting Adaptive Teacher-driven Knowledge Distillation framework (A2T-KD), which aims to balance teacher adaptation and pretraining-knowledge retention. The proposed framework integrates three modules: MITR for cross-epoch representation consistency, DSDO for prediction-space decoupling and class discriminability, and SGKD for feature- and logit-level knowledge transfer. Across nine medical imaging datasets, A2T-KD achieved higher mean values than the fixed-teacher Vanilla KD baseline in 30 of 36 dataset–metric comparisons. It also exhibited the lowest pretraining-set ACC degradation among the evaluated teacher-update baselines on all nine datasets, supporting the intended balance between teacher adaptation and pretraining-knowledge retention under the evaluated settings.

title: Theory of Agent: The Science of Internalization and Externalization for LLM-Based Agents
abstract: A large language model (LLM) agent is a model coupled to a harness: parametric weights that hold knowledge and reasoning ability, wrapped in an external apparatus of memory, tools, and orchestration through which the model perceives and acts. Progress over the past years has come from pushing on both, with stronger models and richer harnesses, but the design decision that quietly governs an agent’s behavior is where competence should live: which knowledge, skills, and control to internalize into the model’s parameters, and which to externalize onto the surrounding harness. These decisions increasingly determine whether an agent is reliable, efficient, and able to keep improving. We investigate this core problem through the lens of the Theory of Agent (ToA), which views an LLM agent not as a task executor but as an epistemic decision-maker in terms of reasoning or acting at every step. The two means it has for that epistemic uncertainty reduction, namely reasoning over what it already holds and acting on the world to obtain what it does not, are the run-time faces of internalization and externalization: reasoning draws on competence that has been absorbed into the model, while acting exploits competence that remains in the harness. We review this internalization and externalization across five chapters. Foundations sets up the basic picture: an agent that, at each step, decides whether to answer from what it already knows or reach outside for what it does not, and what separates a good version of that decision from a wasteful one. Learning examines how training places competence on either side of the boundary, spanning internalization of memory, reasoning, tool-use policy, and world models, and externalization of memory, skills, and orchestration. Aligning treats calibration as the connecting thread across an agent’s cognitive boundaries, efficiency constraints, human preferences, environment constraints, and other agents. Evolving studies how agents revise both sides of the boundary over time, from model-side and harness-side updates to agent–environment co-evolution. Evaluation reinterprets metrics and benchmarks by the epistemic effort they expose and argues for measuring the boundary decision rather than task completion alone. We conclude with the open problems that follow once internalization and externalization are treated as the governing axis of agent design.

title: Focusing on Individual Risk: Personality-Based Content Adaptation in Virtual Agents for Safety Education
abstract: In intelligent virtual agents (IVAs), adaptation strategies based on individual user characteristics are important for enhancing the effectiveness of educational and behavior change interventions. However, prior research on personality-based adaptation in IVAs has predominantly focused on adapting how information is delivered—such as persuasion strategies and communication styles—while the approach of adapting what to focus on, that is, shifting the content focus itself according to individual characteristics, remains underexplored. In this study, we propose a personality-adapted IVA for safety education that shifts the focus of accident analysis information according to users’ personality-based risk profiles. The dialogue structure incorporates user-driven reasoning about accident causes and action planning to support active processing of the focused information. We conducted a field experiment with 74 employees of a power company, assigning participants to either an adaptive condition, which presented personality-focused information, or a control condition, which presented general safety information, over six dialogue sessions spanning three weeks. Comparing pre- and post-intervention importance ratings of accident causes corresponding to each participant’s targeted personality trait, we found that only the importance ratings for the targeted trait selectively increased in the adaptive condition, while no changes were observed for non-targeted traits or in the control condition. This selective pattern demonstrates that shifting content focus according to individual risk factors is an effective IVA adaptation strategy for promoting users’ recognition of accident risks linked to their own personality traits. Furthermore, these findings suggest that content focusing in IVAs can serve as a means of helping users identify and become aware of their own internal states—cognitive and behavioral tendencies—that are relevant to specific outcomes.

title: Examining How Explanations from Multiple AI Agents Affect User Trust After AI Refusal
abstract: AI systems are designed to decline certain requests to avoid providing harmful or inaccurate information. However, refusals can unintentionally reduce users’ impressions of and trust in AI. Prior work has examined what an AI should explain when refusing a request, but offers no guidance on which AI should deliver the explanation when multiple agents are involved. Using a multi-agent scenario, we compared two explanation conditions, delegated explanation by a third-party AI on behalf of the primary AI and shared explanation by both AIs, against two complementary baselines: no explanation and self-explanation by the primary AI. Results showed that users’ impressions of the primary AI dropped when it delegated the explanation about the refusal to the third-party AI. Moreover, this negative impression transferred to the third-party AI: even without directly refusing, it was perceived as reinforcing the primary AI’s refusal. We discuss challenges and opportunities in designing multi-agent AI explanations for refusing users’ requests.

Moreover, this negative impression transferred to the third-party AI: even without directly refusing, it was perceived as reinforcing the primary AI’s refusal. We discuss challenges and opportunities in designing multi-agent AI explanations for refusing users’ requests.

title: AI Cautionary Guide: Pitfalls and Strategies for the Use of Machine Learning in Medical Research
abstract: Machine learning (ML) is increasingly utilized in medical research. However, underrecognized methodological pitfalls can result in misleading conclusions, which if acted upon can result in patient mismanagement and harm. As a result, we have provided a compilation of common pitfalls and practical safeguard considerations for ML-enabled medical research. Examples emphasize the importance of integrating clinical/biologic knowledge and statistical/epidemiologic principles, illustrated with key case examples. Topics include (1) Data drift, which can create artificial trends when coding systems or clinical practices change over time; (2) Feature construction that should be clinically grounded, as models may otherwise learn operational proxies rather than true biology; (3) Accidental data leakage, which can inflate apparent model performance and collapse on real-world deployment; (4) Competing risks and differential time-at-risk that can generate spurious associations in safety analyses if not modeled explicitly; (5) Confounding and collider bias, which can distort findings, particularly in EHR-based studies; (6) For rare outcomes, inappropriate evaluation measures can overstate performance and mislead explainability analyses; (7) Finally, pooled multi-trial analyses require careful handling of the intrinsic heterogeneity to avoid extracting study artifacts rather than generalizable signals. By outlining many of the common potential issues, with lessons learned, we aim to provide the medical and research community with practical insights to help foster trustworthy ML-enabled medical research.

title: Candidate Comparability Before Promotion: Conditional Validation in Adaptive Network Intrusion Detection
abstract: Adaptive network intrusion detection systems retrain classifiers after drift alarms, but an alarm detects change; it does not establish that a challenger should replace the deployed incumbent. Promotion is security-relevant because it changes the model responsible for subsequent attack detection, and evaluating it has a methodological problem: promotion conclusions may depend on how the challenger was constructed and on how much evidence supports it. We test that dependence on CICIDS2017, UNSW-NB15 and ToN-IoT with self-contained challenger pipelines, nested candidate-size controls, a common-harness comparison of nine update policies, and a final sensitivity confining every exact feature vector to one evaluation, training or probe role. Incumbent-owned frozen preprocessing amplified apparent promotion harm; with self-contained challenger pipelines the mean full-drift harm did not persist. Raising nominal candidate evidence from 512 to 2,000 samples per class improved promotion under pool-constructed progressive drift by +0.53, +1.67 and +0.38 balanced-accuracy points: positive and statistically resolved in all three benchmarks, but materially benchmark-dependent rather than homogeneous, and driven mainly by fewer false positives. Policy conclusions were partially robust: policy ordering changed with candidate comparability, no policy globally dominated, and earlier compatibility statements for a label-free estimator and a calibrated ensemble narrowed. Validation helped evidence-disadvantaged challengers but added no average benefit at parity. Thirteen replays on real, time-ordered traffic showed no net harm from always deploying. Challenger construction and evidence should be controlled, reported and interpreted explicitly when promotion is evaluated.

title: STARS-GS: Structure-Aware Regularized Gaussian Splatting for Large-Scale Aerial Surface Reconstruction
abstract: Large-scale 3D surface reconstruction from aerial imagery is fundamental to geospatial mapping and urban modeling. Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have demonstrated considerable potential for this task. However, existing methods still face three major challenges in large and complex scenes: scene partitioning may split continuous scene elements across independently optimized sub-regions; geometric constraints mainly focus on the attributes of individual Gaussians while overlooking their local organization; and uniform regularization struggles to accommodate heterogeneous geometric structures. To address these issues, we propose STARS-GS, a structure-aware 3DGS framework for large-scale surface reconstruction. First, we introduce a structure-aware scene partitioning strategy that better preserves continuous scene structures during partitioning and reduces cross-region geometric inconsistencies and stitching artifacts through boundary refinement. Second, we develop neighborhood-aware Gaussian organization that extends geometric constraints from individual primitives to their neighborhood organization, encouraging Gaussians to better conform to local surface geometry. Third, we introduce adaptive surface regularization that adjusts the regularization strength according to local geometric characteristics, promoting geometric consistency in structured regions while preserving plausible variations in unstructured regions. Extensive experiments on large-scale aerial photogrammetry benchmarks demonstrate that STARS-GS consistently outperforms the evaluated Gaussian-based methods in surface reconstruction. It increases the average F1-score from 0.640 for the second-best method to 0.698, corresponding to a relative improvement of approximately 9.1\%, demonstrating effective improvements in geometric accuracy and surface completeness.

title: PACodec: A Low-bitrate Neural Speech Codec with Parallel Additive Vector Quantization
abstract: This paper proposes PACodec, a novel low-bitrate neural speech codec based on parallel additive vector quantization (PAVQ). Unlike the mainstream residual vector quantization (RVQ) used in most neural speech codecs, where vector quantizers (VQs) are sequentially dependent, the PAVQ strategy adopted in PACodec aggregates parallel quantization results to optimize bitrate usage. Specifically, the PAVQ adopts a "global-local-global" (GLG) design: the global encoded features are quantized in parallel by multiple independent VQs, each attending to a local component of the representation, and their outputs are aggregated through addition to yield the final global quantization result for decoding. Experimental results show that PACodec, as each VQ focuses only on local information, supports smaller codebooks and reduces bitrate by 30% compared with baselines at the same decoding quality, with only minor model complexity. Further analysis shows that, owing to the GLG framework of PAVQ, the proposed PACodec is disentanglement-friendly, and each independent VQ captures different aspects of speech, e.g., content, timbre, and acoustic details, suggesting potential for application to downstream tasks such as voice conversion.

title: LAR-OS: Autonomous Multi-Agent AI Operating System & Unified Antigravity Gateway
abstract: LAR-OS (Language Agent Research Operating System) v3.0.0 is an open-source, enterprise-grade autonomous multi-agent engineering operating system and unified AI gateway. Core Capabilities: Bidirectional Anthropic ↔ Gemini Tool-Calling Translation: Enables Claude Code CLI and Anthropic-native tools to execute multi-step autonomous loops through Google Gemini 2.5 Flash / Pro engines with zero code changes. Antigravity ↔ Jules Multi-Agent Delegation: Implements a strict hierarchical orchestration architecture (User → Antigravity Chief Orchestrator → Jules Delegated Worker Pool → GitHub / Hugging Face Source of Truth) with automated code review under Anti-Crash Protocol (ACP-V1). Distributed Multi-Node Compute: Pools multi-account Google AI Pro credentials and SSH Linux Cloud Shell nodes with dynamic round-robin failover and smart cooldown. RTK Context Compactor & Bounded LRU Cache: Reduces token overhead by 35% and accelerates prompt turnaround time while protecting against memory exhaustion. Continuous Knowledge Sync: Automated bi-directional synchronization across Google Drive for PC, Obsidian Vault, and NotebookLM.

title: Dynamic Graph Theory-based Adaptive Optimization Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic graph theory-based optimization algorithm designed to improve the speed and quality of optimization processes. Traditional optimization methods often rely on static graph structures, which can limit the algorithm's effectiveness. We propose a method that dynamically modifies the graph structure during the optimization process, creating a more efficient representation of the problem. This adaptation allows the algorithm to effectively navigate complex landscapes and find optimal solutions more rapidly. The core mechanism involves analyzing the problem's structure and adjusting the graph to enhance connectivity and reduce the search space. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through simulations and illustrative examples, showcasing significant improvements in solution speed and quality compared to existing optimization techniques.

title: Quantum Topology for Quantum Computing Algorithm Optimization
abstract: Quantum topology, a novel field of physics, offers a unique approach to manipulating quantum states and exploring complex quantum phenomena. This paper explores the potential of quantum topology to revolutionize algorithm optimization within the realm of quantum computing. We propose a new algorithmic framework, 'Quantum Topology Optimization', predicated on the principles of quantum topology to enhance the efficiency and performance of various quantum algorithms. The core mechanism leverages the inherent properties of quantum topology to guide the optimization process, leading to significant improvements in computational outcomes. The paper details the theoretical underpinnings, implementation considerations, and preliminary results demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach. We conclude with a discussion of the challenges and future directions of this research.

title: 自适应时空几何的量子模拟验证
abstract: This paper investigates the application of self-adaptive spacetime geometry in quantum simulation verification. Traditional quantum simulation validation often relies on static parameter adjustments, limiting accuracy and efficiency. We propose a novel framework that dynamically adjusts simulation parameters based on the results of the simulation, leading to improved accuracy and reduced computational cost. The core mechanism involves utilizing self-adaptive spacetime geometry to iteratively refine the simulation's parameters, optimizing for verification accuracy. This approach addresses the limitations of static validation methods by providing a continuous feedback loop. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework through a series of simulations focusing on verifying the properties of a simplified quantum system. The study highlights the potential of this approach to significantly enhance the reliability and speed of quantum simulation verification.

title: 基于自适应的梯度下降算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel gradient descent algorithm, termed "Adaptive Gradient Descent" (AGD), designed to enhance convergence speed and robustness. Traditional gradient descent frequently operates on a uniform learning rate and momentum, leading to suboptimal optimization and susceptibility to local minima. AGD dynamically adjusts the learning rate and momentum based on the local gradient landscape, intelligently prioritizing areas with higher curvature and minimizing the risk of getting stuck in suboptimal solutions. This paper details the algorithm's core mechanism, including the gradient landscape adaptation process and its resulting benefits in terms of faster convergence and improved robustness. We present a comprehensive analysis of the algorithm's performance on various benchmark datasets and demonstrate its superior results compared to established gradient descent methods.

title: Quantum Privacy via Entanglement Decoherence
abstract: This paper investigates the utilization of entanglement decoherence as a novel privacy-preserving mechanism within quantum computation. The core concept hinges on strategically introducing controlled decoherence into quantum calculations, thereby mitigating the risk of information leakage and facilitating secure quantum processing. Traditional approaches to quantum privacy often rely on complex cryptographic protocols, which can introduce significant overhead and limitations. This research proposes a fundamentally different method leveraging the inherent properties of entanglement and its susceptibility to decoherence. Specifically, we explore techniques for introducing precisely calibrated decoherence effects to obscure the intermediate quantum states, effectively limiting the information accessible to potential eavesdroppers. The theoretical framework presented outlines the key mathematical relationships and operational considerations for achieving this goal, focusing on the probabilistic reduction of information leakage. The proposed model offers a potentially more efficient and scalable approach to quantum privacy, addressing some of the challenges associated with existing solutions. We define key parameters such as decoherence rate (Γ), initial entanglement fidelity (F₀), and the degree of controlled decoherence (δ) to quantify the effectiveness of the privacy protection. The work culminates in a discussion of the trade-offs between privacy and computational utility, highlighting the need for careful parameter optimization.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Geometric Simulation of Non-Linear Systems
abstract: Quantum-enhanced geometric simulation aims to revolutionize the modeling of complex, non-linear systems by leveraging the unique properties of quantum mechanics. This paper explores the potential of utilizing quantum entanglement to stabilize and improve the accuracy of geometric simulations, addressing key challenges in current computational methods. We introduce a novel quantum algorithm designed to enhance the fidelity of geometric representations, offering a pathway to more robust and insightful simulations. The paper details the theoretical framework, the algorithm's implementation, and preliminary experimental results demonstrating the algorithm's effectiveness in simulating specific non-linear systems. The core claim is that entanglement provides a transformative means to overcome limitations inherent in classical geometric simulation, leading to significant improvements in stability and accuracy.

title: Symbolic Regression with Genetic Programming and Temporal Constraints
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to symbolic regression that leverages genetic programming (GP) and explicitly incorporates temporal constraints. Traditional symbolic regression methods often struggle to effectively model dynamic systems, where variables change over time. Our method addresses this limitation by evolving a population of symbolic expressions, guided by temporal operators such as difference, integration, and convolution, which force the resulting equations to represent time-dependent relationships. The core claim is to perform symbolic regression using genetic programming, incorporating temporal constraints to identify equations that accurately model dynamic systems. The proposed mechanism evolves a population of symbolic expressions, applying temporal operators to constrain the generated equations to represent time-dependent relationships. The results demonstrate the ability to discover equations that accurately capture time-varying phenomena, offering a significant advancement in the field of symbolic regression. This work provides a robust and adaptable framework for equation discovery from time-series data.

title: Quantum Information Field Theory: A Non-Euclidean Analysis
abstract: Quantum Information Field Theory (QIFT) represents a novel theoretical framework for understanding and manipulating quantum information, particularly concerning its inherent non-Euclidean properties. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of QIFT, demonstrating its unique characteristics and potential for advanced quantum computation. We establish a new theoretical model, rigorously exploring how non-Euclidean structures influence quantum systems. The core mechanism centers on leveraging the non-Euclidean properties to optimize quantum algorithms, ultimately proposing a new class of algorithms specifically designed to exploit this phenomenon. This work aims to push the boundaries of quantum computation by establishing a robust, mathematically-grounded approach to non-Euclidean quantum systems.

title: Non-Homogeneous Data-Driven Distributed Knowledge Graph Construction
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to constructing distributed knowledge graphs from non-homogeneous data sources, encompassing text, images, and videos. The core idea revolves around leveraging deep learning models for data embedding to capture semantic relationships and subsequently utilizing distributed storage and computation technologies to build scalable knowledge graphs. The challenges inherent in integrating diverse data types into a unified knowledge representation are addressed, resulting in a method that significantly improves both the quality and coverage of the generated knowledge graphs. The proposed system emphasizes adaptability and resilience through its distributed architecture, making it suitable for handling increasingly complex and heterogeneous data landscapes. The key contributions lie in the seamless fusion of deep learning embeddings with distributed graph technologies, offering a practical solution for knowledge graph construction in real-world scenarios. The system's architecture and methodology are detailed, outlining the data ingestion, embedding, graph construction, and scalability aspects. Experimental results (though not presented through formal experiments due to the nature of the approach) demonstrate the potential of this method in creating robust and informative knowledge graphs.

title: Nonlinear Topological Geometry Quantum Computation Validation Framework
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum computation validation framework leveraging the inherent non-linearity of topological geometry and the quantum entanglement mechanism. We propose a new approach to quantum algorithm verification, focusing on dynamically computing and analyzing topological states. The core concept is the "拓扑量子态" – a quantum state intrinsically linked to topological structure, allowing for precise validation of quantum algorithms through their dynamic evolution. This research utilizes dynamic quantum state manipulation to test and verify the correctness and stability of quantum computations. We demonstrate the framework's efficacy through a series of simulations and analyses, showcasing its potential to improve the reliability of quantum algorithms.

This research aims to provide a fundamentally new approach to understanding and analyzing phase transitions, promising increased efficiency and accuracy in identifying these critical phenomena.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Based Distributed Neural Network Synchronization
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to neural network synchronization leveraging the phenomenon of quantum entanglement. We propose a distributed neural network architecture where synchronization is achieved instantaneously through entanglement, bypassing the limitations imposed by the speed of light and the inherent delays in conventional neural network communication. The core concept involves integrating quantum processors and classical processors within each neuron. Quantum processors, utilizing entangled states, provide real-time synchronization of other neurons, while classical processors manage classical information exchange and feedback. The proposed method represents a significant departure from existing synchronization techniques, which rely on finite-speed signal transmission. This research has the potential to revolutionize both biological and computational neural networks by enabling truly instantaneous synchronization. We present a detailed theoretical framework and explore the key components of this system, focusing on the operational mechanisms and potential challenges. The ultimate goal is to demonstrate a viable pathway for constructing a synchronized distributed neural network based on the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics.

We propose a distributed neural network architecture where synchronization is achieved instantaneously through entanglement, bypassing the limitations imposed by the speed of light and the inherent delays in conventional neural network communication. The core concept involves integrating quantum processors and classical processors within each neuron. Quantum processors, utilizing entangled states, provide real-time synchronization of other neurons, while classical processors manage classical information exchange and feedback. The proposed method represents a significant departure from existing synchronization techniques, which rely on finite-speed signal transmission. This research has the potential to revolutionize both biological and computational neural networks by enabling truly instantaneous synchronization. We present a detailed theoretical framework and explore the key components of this system, focusing on the operational mechanisms and potential challenges. The ultimate goal is to demonstrate a viable pathway for constructing a synchronized distributed neural network based on the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics.

title: 基于量子拓扑的自适应量子计算量子子图优化
abstract: Quantum computing is a rapidly advancing field with the potential to revolutionize various industries through its unique computational capabilities. However, achieving high-performance quantum algorithms requires careful optimization of quantum circuits, particularly the design of quantum state vectors, which is currently a significant bottleneck. This paper introduces a novel approach to quantum state vector optimization leveraging the principles of quantum topology. We propose a method that dynamically adjusts the quantum state by exploiting the inherent topological properties of the quantum system, resulting in improved accuracy and efficiency in various quantum computing tasks. The core mechanism centers around constructing and manipulating quantum states through a carefully orchestrated topological transformation, offering a fundamentally different perspective on optimization compared to existing methods. This work demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach through theoretical analysis and preliminary experimental validation, showcasing its potential to significantly enhance quantum computation.

title: Title: Geometric Fractal Regularization for Machine Learning
abstract: This paper investigates the application of geometric fractal regularization to enhance the generalization performance of machine learning models. Traditional regularization techniques often rely on simple patterns, which can be brittle and fail to capture the inherent complexity of the data. We propose a novel approach that leverages the principles of fractal geometry to introduce self-organizing patterns within the model's architecture, aiming to generate more robust feature representations. The core mechanism involves designing a pattern that dynamically adapts to the data distribution, promoting better separation between training and test sets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique through experimental results on several benchmark datasets, showing improved generalization performance compared to existing regularization methods. This work contributes to a more robust and adaptive approach to model training, potentially leading to more reliable and accurate machine learning systems.

title: Symbolic Simulation of Complex Biological Systems using Agent-Based Modeling and Neural Networks
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to simulating complex biological systems by integrating agent-based modeling (ABM) with neural networks. Traditional simulation methods often fail to accurately represent the emergent behaviors arising from intricate interactions within biological systems. Our methodology addresses this limitation by constructing an ABM where individual biological agents operate according to defined rules, and employs neural networks to dynamically learn and adapt to the system's evolving behavior. The core of our approach lies in the synergistic combination of these two techniques, allowing for a more nuanced and realistic representation of biological phenomena. We demonstrate the potential of this combined approach through a conceptual framework, outlining the key components and their interactions, and highlighting the advantages over conventional simulation methods. This work provides a foundation for future research into complex biological system modeling and offers a pathway towards a deeper understanding of biological processes.

title: Quantum-Inspired Optimization with Adaptive Kernel Functions
abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm, Quantum-Inspired Optimization with Adaptive Kernel Functions, designed to enhance the efficiency of complex optimization problems. We leverage quantum-inspired kernel functions to guide the evolution of the optimization process, fostering faster convergence and improving solution quality. The algorithm's core mechanism centers around dynamically adapting kernel parameters to navigate the problem space, mimicking the principles of quantum mechanics. This adaptation is achieved through a self-tuning process that continuously evaluates the impact of each kernel parameter on the optimization landscape. The paper explores the potential benefits of this approach, particularly in scenarios involving high dimensionality and complex non-convex functions, and presents preliminary results demonstrating improved performance compared to traditional optimization methods.

title: 基于动态的自适应的隐马尔可夫模型
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to probabilistic modeling based on dynamic adaptive Markov Models (DAMMs). Traditional Markov Models often rely on static condition distributions, offering limited flexibility and potential for suboptimal prediction accuracy. We propose a dynamic adjustment mechanism that iteratively refines the model's condition distribution based on observed data, significantly enhancing predictive performance. The core contribution lies in the utilization of a feedback loop that continuously adjusts the distribution to minimize prediction errors, resulting in improved model robustness and generalization. We explore the effectiveness of this dynamic adaptation through simulation and preliminary analysis, demonstrating significant gains in accuracy across a range of scenarios.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic topology algorithm based on quantum entanglement, designed to optimize complex systems through adaptive topology manipulation. The core of this algorithm leverages the unique properties of entangled quantum states to dynamically adjust the topology of a system, offering a significant advancement over traditional static optimization techniques. We detail the algorithm's methodology, the underlying quantum principles, and its potential applications across diverse fields. The paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the algorithm's performance, demonstrating its efficacy in solving complex optimization problems.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Gradient Descent for Machine Learning
abstract: This paper explores the integration of quantum mechanics into gradient descent algorithms for machine learning. We propose a novel approach that leverages quantum tunneling to accelerate convergence and utilizes quantum-enhanced sampling to broaden the search space, ultimately aiming to improve the training speed and robustness of machine learning models. The core mechanism involves employing quantum tunneling to guide the gradient updates, while simultaneously utilizing quantum-enhanced sampling techniques to navigate the complex landscape of the search space. This research offers a potential paradigm shift in the training process, potentially unlocking significant advancements in machine learning.

title: 基于图神经网络的动态系统优化算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic system optimization algorithm based on graph neural networks (GNNs). Traditional optimization methods often struggle with dynamic systems due to their static nature, requiring manual adjustments and potentially leading to suboptimal solutions. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) offer a powerful framework for representing and analyzing system relationships, allowing for automated learning and optimization. We propose a GNN-based approach that dynamically models system dependencies, learns optimal system structures, and facilitates efficient optimization. The algorithm's core mechanism involves constructing a graph representation of the system, leveraging GNNs to propagate information and learn optimal node connections, ultimately leading to improved performance. This work demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach through simulations and initial analysis, showcasing significant improvements in complex system optimization tasks.

title: Probability Algebra of Quantum States: A Novel Approach to Quantum Computing and Information Processing
abstract: Quantum state representation is fundamental to modern quantum computing and information processing, but its inherent complexities often necessitate sophisticated mathematical models. This paper investigates the potential of leveraging probability algebra to address these challenges by introducing a novel framework for quantifying quantum state non-linear relationships. The core principle centers around a "correlation function" built upon probability distributions, facilitating a dynamic interaction between the state's probability distribution and the underlying algebraic structure. This framework aims to improve the precision of quantum calculations and information processing by providing a more intuitive and robust representation of quantum phenomena. The investigation explores the potential benefits of this approach and outlines preliminary results demonstrating the framework's efficacy.

title: Quantum States: An Adaptive Space
abstract: Quantum states represent the fundamental building blocks of quantum information, exhibiting inherent uncertainty and sensitivity to external influences. Traditional approaches to managing these states often rely on pre-defined parameters and static control schemes, limiting their adaptability to complex and dynamic environments. This paper introduces a novel quantum state space – the Adaptive Space of Quantum States – designed to automatically adjust quantum states based on computational goals and environmental noise, ultimately fostering more efficient and robust quantum computation. The core mechanism centers around a dynamic space construction, coupled with quantum error correction for optimized parameter adaptation. This offers a significant advancement over existing methods, enabling quantum algorithms to respond to changing conditions with unprecedented precision.

title: The Anthropomorphism Paradox in AI Chatbots: A Review of Consumer Trust and Brand Relationship Outcomes
abstract: Anthropomorphic chatbot design is reshaping how businesses engage consumers by bringing perceived humanity to digital service encounters. This review synthesizes recent theoretical and empirical work on how anthropomorphic characteristics in chatbots shape consumer trust and brand relationship quality (BRQ). Drawing on anthropomorphism theory, relationship marketing theory, and the Computers-Are-Social-Actors (CASA) paradigm, it examines the roles of perceived authenticity, comfort, social presence, and engagement in shaping consumer responses to human-like conversational agents. The reviewed evidence suggests that moderate anthropomorphism, expressed through warmth, personalization, responsiveness, and natural language, tends to increase trust, satisfaction, engagement, and emotional connection with a brand, while excessive human-likeness can trigger discomfort, privacy concerns, unrealistic expectations, and an erosion of trust, consistent with the uncanny valley effect. The review further highlights that these effects are highly context-dependent, and that transparent or hybrid chatbot designs may help preserve emotional connection while retaining functional credibility. The paper closes with a synthesis of theoretical, managerial, and future-research implications for brand managers designing AI-mediated customer touchpoints.

title: Cryptography
abstract: This chapter provides an overview of cryptographic principles, emphasizing their role in maintaining data confidentiality through encryption and key management. It distinguishes cryptography from steganography, noting that while cryptography secures content, it does not conceal the presence of communication. Also, it explains hash functions and their use for integrity verification and in digital signatures for authentication. Finally, it illuminates the necessary security groundwork for the covert communication framework proposed in this research.

title: Rollcast: Proper-Score Gated Rolling Anchors for Adaptive Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting
abstract: Rollcast is a probabilistic forecasting method for univariate time series that combines a compact set of rolling statistical anchors rather than relying on a single global model. Rolling means, medians, extrema, regression endpoints, and quantiles define candidate forecast locations and a representation of the current state. A state-dependent softmax gate learns anchor probabilities by minimizing negative log predictive density, while residual distributions retrieved from similar historical states provide local uncertainty. Recursive simulation propagates the resulting mixture over multiple forecast horizons. The method is evaluated in a Monte Carlo study covering eight data-generating processes, including autoregressive, random-walk, local-trend, threshold, regime-switching, stochastic-volatility, heavy-tailed, and variance-break dynamics. Across 2,000 independent fitted series, Rollcast is compared with the true conditional predictive distribution generated by an oracle simulator. Overall empirical coverage is 86.2% for nominal 90% intervals and 91.5% for nominal 95% intervals. Predictive intervals are on average 13.6% wider than the oracle at the 90% level, while CRPS is 14.4% higher than oracle CRPS. Performance is closest to the oracle under autoregressive, threshold, stochastic-volatility, heavy-tailed, and variance-break dynamics, while local trends and regime switching are more challenging. The results indicate that Rollcast can construct competitive probabilistic forecasts from simple, interpretable local summaries, while also identifying limitations in calibration and recursive uncertainty propagation.

title: The Blind Spot in 2D Infants' Pose Estimation:Robust Learning from Noisy Annotations
abstract: Noisy annotations pose a significant challenge for supervised deep learning, as neural networks rely on large-scale, high-quality labeled data whose corruption can severely impair model performance. Although robustness to label noise has been extensively studied for classification tasks, it remains relatively underexplored in Pose Estimation (PE). This limitation becomes critical in clinical contexts, including neonatology, where PE of preterm infants is used to support the assessment of spontaneous motility, a key indicator of neurodevelopmental trajectories. In such settings, infants' images labeling is further hindered by visual challenges (e.g., keypoint self-occlusions, caregiver interference), making the annotation process inherently susceptible to errors. To tackle noisy annotations in PE, we introduce REliable keypoint selection via Memory of traINing Dynamics (REMIND), a clustering-based keypoint-selection strategy that exploits keypoint-wise training dynamics to identify noisy labels without assuming any prior knowledge of the noise distribution, thus enabling noise-free model training. When evaluated on the proprietary NeoPose dataset, comprising 46 videos of 46 preterm infants recorded in real clinical settings, REMIND correctly identifies noisy annotations across multiple corruption scenarios, achieving up to 93\% Area Under the Curve (AUC) with three different PE architectures used in the relevant literature. To our knowledge, this is the first study to explicitly address label noise in preterm infants' PE, paving the way for the design of trustworthy learning-based algorithms for infants'monitoring support when data quality cannot be guaranteed.

title: Inferring Hidden User Models from the Behavior of Personalized LLM Agents
abstract: Recent personalized LLM agents increasingly transform information retained in memory into compressed or structured representations, which we call user models, to guide later decisions. When source wording is removed from the state reachable through the ordinary interface, these models are commonly treated as more privacy-preserving because direct memory-extraction attacks lose the text they target. Yet we argue that user models expose a new attack surface because an attacker can still recover the private information from the personalized choices they shape, even when source records and backend state remain inaccessible. We therefore introduce UMPeek, a black-box attack based on hypothesis-guided adaptive probing to infer such hidden user model. It forms hypotheses from choices left open by a request, switches among ordinary follow-up tasks, and retains only claims supported and not contradicted by visible behavior. We conduct an extensive benchmark evaluation across diverse personalization tasks and user-model backends against existing attacks. We further validate UMPeek in real-world systems using information confirmed to be retained, and we evaluate defenses against its adaptive probing. Overall, UMPeek outperforms existing attacks in both benchmark and real-world comparisons and continues to recover user information under response-level defenses, showing that keeping records and backend state inaccessible does not guarantee semantic privacy when retained information shapes visible behavior.

title: SignSeek: Learning Transferable Representations for Sign Dictionary Retrieval
abstract: Sign language dictionaries are essential resources for sign language learners, yet automatically retrieving a sign from a dictionary, given only a query video, remains a challenging problem due to the natural variability between signers. Existing sign representation learning methods are built for closed-set recognition, producing embeddings that do not generalise to the open-set, signer-independent setting that retrieval demands. \textbf{SignSeek} closes this gap by contrastively learning sign representations with saliency-guided articulator masking. A contrastive objective aligns same-gloss signs across signers, while our Articulator Saliency-Guided Masking (ASGM) pinpoints the single most critical articulator per sign. This drives two complementary objectives, a masked contrastive alignment (MAC) loss that sees the sign through a single articulator and a masked prediction (MAP) loss that reconstructs it in latent space from the surrounding spatio-temporal context. Pretrained on 266K samples ($\sim$5,700 glosses) across multiple sign languages, \textbf{SignSeek} sets a new state-of-the-art performance in cross-corpus retrieval on ASL-Citizen, WLASL, and NMFs-CSL without any downstream fine-tuning. Strikingly, it achieves zero-shot generalisation to an entirely unseen British Sign Language (BSL), surpassing methods explicitly trained on BSL, and transfers seamlessly to isolated sign recognition and subtitle alignment, outperforming prior skeleton-based methods.

title: Preserving Knowledge across Space and Time for Continual Video Deepfake Detection
abstract: The continuous emergence of high-quality video deepfakes requires detectors that continually adapt to new forgery patterns, yet existing approaches, which are designed for deepfake images, fail to capture video-specific cues. Unlike deepfake images that contain only spatial artifacts, deepfake videos leave distinct evidence along both spatial and temporal axes, necessitating the separate preservation of each modality during sequential model updates. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a continual deepfake video detection framework, Modality-Specific Frequency Distillation (MSFD), that explicitly decomposes video features into spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal modalities in the frequency domain. This decomposition enables independent preservation of each modality, as different deepfake video types exhibit varying reliance on spatial and temporal cues across tasks. Furthermore, MSFD adopts a cross-modality decorrelation loss that encourages spatiotemporal representations to remain orthogonal to single-modality cues. Extensive experiments show that our framework achieves stronger adaptation and preserves performance more effectively than state-of-the-art methods across diverse continual deepfake video scenarios.

title: AI Tourism Service-Use Breadth and Perceived-Benefit Breadth
abstract: Aims: This study examines whether broader use of AI-enabled tourism service categories is associated with recognition of a wider range of perceived benefits after age and travel frequency are taken into account. Study Design: A cross-sectional secondary analysis was conducted using a predefined data-collection window from an ongoing online AI tourism survey project. Place and Duration of Study: The survey was administered online through Tencent Questionnaire. Responses collected between April 1 and June 27, 2026, were included in the present analysis. Methodology: The analytical sample comprised 496 valid responses. Two formative category-count measures were constructed: the AI Use Index (0–5), representing AI tourism service-use breadth, and the Positive Index (0–4), representing perceived-benefit breadth. Hierarchical linear regression was used as the primary analytical approach, with age and travel frequency included as control variables. Ordered logistic regression and sensitivity analyses using an alternative benefit measure and the exclusion of contradictory multiple-choice responses were conducted to assess the stability of the main association. Results: Adding the AI Use Index increased the explained variance in the Positive Index from 7.6% to 33.7% (ΔR² = .261). AI service-use breadth was positively associated with perceived-benefit breadth after age and travel frequency were taken into account (B = 0.481, 95% CI [0.413, 0.549], P < .001). evidence.abstract: Aims: This study examines whether broader use of AI-enabled tourism service categories is associated with recognition of a wider range of perceived benefits after age and travel frequency are taken into account. title: Towards Secure AI How far can international standards take us?
abstract: This CETaS Research Report prepares policymakers to understand and address the significant cybersecurity challenges that have resulted from the widespread rollout of AI, with a specific focus on the role played by international standards. Our findings indicate that many of the challenges associated with securing AI systems are not new and can be resolved by updating existing cybersecurity standards. However, several challenges are new and evolving rapidly, such as those relating to the security of AI supply chains and new threats which have emerged in the context of generative AI. Standards development organisations (SDOs) have begun to introduce international standards which help protect AI systems from attack, but these standards are at a nascent stage. We recommend governments redouble their efforts to support SDOs and to ensure crucial international standards are made available and accessible to those who need to implement them. We also recommend further investment in related research to advance understandings of adversarial AI, ensuring that future international standards don’t just focus on identifying vulnerabilities, but instead offer robust and specific mitigation strategies.

title: 基于自适应的联邦学习算法
abstract: This paper investigates the challenges and opportunities presented by federated learning in dynamic environments. Traditional federated learning approaches often rely on fixed network topology and data distribution, leading to suboptimal model performance and inefficient data utilization. We propose a novel self-adaptive federated learning algorithm that dynamically adjusts model parameters and data sharing strategies based on network topology and data distribution, addressing these limitations. The core mechanism involves a dynamically evolving network structure and a sophisticated adaptive weighting scheme. This framework aims to improve model generalization, reduce communication costs, and enhance data privacy. We present a rigorous theoretical analysis and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm through simulations and experiments. The key innovations lie in the algorithm's ability to continuously re-evaluate the network topology and data distribution, adapting to real-time changes.

title: Title: Quantum Bayesian Neural Networks for Ensemble Learning
abstract: Quantum Bayesian Neural Networks (QBNNs) represent a novel approach to neural network architecture, integrating quantum superposition and entanglement to enhance ensemble learning performance, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional data. This paper explores the potential of QBNNs to overcome the limitations of classical ensembles by leveraging quantum phenomena for improved representation, processing, and generalization. We detail the design of a QBNN framework, focusing on the interplay between quantum states, Bayesian inference, and ensemble aggregation. The core claim centers on the design of a QBNN that utilizes quantum superposition and entanglement to achieve significantly enhanced accuracy and robustness in ensemble learning scenarios. The paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the theoretical and practical implications of this approach, including mathematical formulations and experimental validation demonstrating improvements over traditional ensemble methods. We discuss the challenges and future directions for this research, emphasizing the potential for transformative advancements in data analysis and machine learning.

title: Quantum-Driven Constraint Optimization for Complex Robotics
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of quantum computing to revolutionize complex robotics, specifically focusing on optimization of robot control and movement. Traditional robotic control systems often struggle with complex environments and constraints, limiting the ability to achieve optimal performance. We propose a novel quantum algorithm designed to address these challenges by leveraging a dynamic, quantum-based simulation of the physical environment to generate constraints. This approach aims to enable robots to navigate and manipulate objects with unprecedented precision and adaptability. The core mechanism centers on utilizing a quantum solver to efficiently explore the search space of possible robot motions, guided by the simulation's feedback. This contrasts with traditional methods, which often struggle with the high dimensionality and complexity of robot dynamics. The research demonstrates the feasibility of this quantum-driven approach through simulations and preliminary experiments, showcasing potential improvements in robot control and movement.

title: Chaos System Simulation based on Quantum Computing
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum computing for simulating chaotic systems. Traditional methods of chaotic system simulation are often limited by the precision and efficiency of classical computation. This research proposes leveraging the unique capabilities of quantum computing, specifically quantum chaos algorithms, to overcome these limitations. The core idea involves utilizing quantum superposition and interference to accurately model the dynamics of chaotic systems. We present a theoretical framework for this approach, outlining the key mathematical formulations and demonstrating how quantum mechanics can provide a more accurate and efficient simulation compared to classical methods. The paper focuses on the theoretical underpinnings and potential benefits, without presenting experimental results. We aim to establish a foundation for future research in this burgeoning field.

abstract: This paper presents a novel system for temporal phase synchronization, aiming to significantly improve the accuracy of quantum simulations by automatically synchronizing the collapse of wave function probabilities across multiple quantum systems. We introduce a dynamic feedback loop algorithm that ensures precise alignment between each quantum system's collapse, thereby minimizing errors and enhancing simulation fidelity. The core mechanism centers on a refined approach to wave function collapse, directly addressing the inherent challenges of multi-system quantum dynamics.

title: Quantum-Inspired Stochastic Gradient Descent with Entangled Noise
abstract: This paper proposes a novel stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm, termed Quantum-Inspired Stochastic Gradient Descent with Entangled Noise (QISGDEN), that draws inspiration from the principles of quantum entanglement to enhance the optimization process. Traditional SGD relies on adding Gaussian noise to the gradient estimates, a technique that can sometimes lead to slow convergence and limited exploration of the loss landscape. QISGDEN addresses this limitation by incorporating correlated noise, modeled after the complex correlations present in entangled quantum states. This approach introduces a more sophisticated exploration strategy, potentially leading to faster convergence rates and improved optimization performance. The algorithm utilizes a modified update rule incorporating a correlation factor that reflects the degree of entanglement, allowing for dynamic adjustment of the noise contribution based on the current state of the optimization. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of the method and present a detailed analysis of its convergence properties. Preliminary results suggest the potential of QISGDEN to outperform standard SGD in certain scenarios, particularly those with complex loss landscapes. The key contribution lies in translating quantum mechanical concepts—specifically entanglement—into a practical optimization framework.

title: Information-Theoretic Proofs of Concept for Neural Network Robustness
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to evaluating the robustness of neural networks by leveraging information-theoretic principles. We move beyond empirical methods, which often rely on black-box evaluations, and establish mathematically rigorous bounds on robustness using concepts like mutual information and entropy. The core idea is to quantify the sensitivity of a neural network's output to small, adversarial perturbations by examining the mutual information between the input and output. This approach provides a foundational framework for understanding and predicting robustness, potentially leading to the design of more resilient neural network architectures and training strategies. We demonstrate the feasibility and utility of this method through theoretical analysis, establishing key relationships and providing a starting point for further research in this critical area. The work focuses on establishing a theoretical understanding of robustness, paving the way for more targeted and effective defense mechanisms against adversarial attacks. ---

title: 基于动态内存的量子计算的自适应量子环境控制
abstract: Quantum computing holds immense promise for revolutionizing fields ranging from drug discovery to materials science. However, achieving practical quantum computation faces significant challenges, primarily concerning the stability and fidelity of quantum states. This paper introduces a novel approach to quantum environment control based on dynamic memory management, designed to dynamically adjust quantum system parameters and enhance quantum computation efficiency. We propose a system that iteratively adjusts parameters based on the observed quantum state, optimizing for reduced error rates and enhanced coherence. The core mechanism leverages a dynamically allocated memory bank to hold quantum state information, allowing for rapid and flexible environmental manipulation. We present a theoretical framework outlining the design, implementation considerations, and potential performance benefits of this approach. We demonstrate the efficacy of our system through simulations illustrating improved coherence and reduced error rates compared to static control methods. This work represents a significant step towards building more robust and versatile quantum computation systems.

title: Bayesian Deep Reinforcement Learning for Robotic Manipulation with Tactile Sensing
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to robotic manipulation leveraging Bayesian deep reinforcement learning (BDRL) and tactile sensing. Traditional deep reinforcement learning (DRL) struggles in uncertain environments due to its reliance on deterministic state representations and action predictions. To address this, we propose an agent architecture that integrates tactile sensor data directly into the state space, allowing the agent to perceive the environment's uncertainty. Furthermore, we employ Bayesian inference within the DRL framework to quantify the uncertainty associated with the agent's actions, leading to more robust and reliable control. The core mechanism involves a deep neural network that learns a policy from the combined tactile and visual input, coupled with a Bayesian network that updates the agent's belief about its actions. Experimental results demonstrate that this BDRL approach significantly improves robotic manipulation performance compared to standard DRL methods, particularly in scenarios with high levels of sensory noise and object variability. The key contributions of this work are the synergistic combination of tactile sensing and BDRL for enhanced uncertainty management and improved robot control.

title: Title: Non-Standard Kernel Matching for Deep Neural Networks
abstract: This paper introduces a novel kernel matching technique designed to enhance the performance of deep neural networks, particularly in scenarios involving complex, high-dimensional datasets. Traditional kernel matching methods often struggle with data heterogeneity and require substantial computational resources. Our approach focuses on developing a more efficient and adaptable comparison process, leveraging a multi-stage evaluation strategy and a dynamically adjusted weighting scheme to mitigate the limitations of existing techniques. We aim to improve the accuracy of deep learning models by providing a robust and adaptable comparison framework. The core mechanism involves a hierarchical comparison process, systematically evaluating different kernel functions to identify the optimal matching for each data point. This enhances the model's ability to generalize to unseen data and improves the overall robustness of the network. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our technique through a series of experiments on benchmark datasets, showcasing significant improvements in accuracy and generalization performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

title: Title: Adaptive Statistical Inference for Complex Systems
abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive statistical inference algorithm designed for complex systems, focusing on dynamic environments characterized by significant noise. Standard Bayesian inference often struggles with high-dimensional data and non-stationary distributions, necessitating the creation of explicit prior specifications. Our approach, termed the Meta-Bayesian Network, dynamically adjusts the complexity of the model based on the observed noise distribution, providing a more robust and adaptable framework. The algorithm's core mechanism involves a meta-Bayesian network that iteratively refines the model's parameters to better represent the system's variability. This results in improved prediction accuracy and a greater capacity to handle complex, evolving data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm through a series of simulations, highlighting its superior performance compared to traditional Bayesian methods in scenarios with substantial noise and high dimensionality.
