title: Dynamic Adaptive Neural Network Attention Optimization
abstract: This paper presents a novel dynamic self-adaptive neural network attention mechanism designed to enhance model performance on long sequences. Traditional attention mechanisms often rely on fixed parameters, limiting their ability to effectively capture crucial information. Our approach dynamically adjusts attention weights, allowing the model to adapt to the characteristics of the input data and reduce computational complexity. The core of this innovation lies in an iterative refinement process that optimizes attention weights based on a learned metric derived from the sequence's structure. This results in a model that exhibits improved long-range dependency modeling, leading to enhanced performance across a range of tasks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this mechanism through extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets, showcasing significant improvements in both accuracy and efficiency.

title: Title: Fractal Self-Similarity for Quantum Algorithm Design
abstract: Fractal self-similarity, a ubiquitous phenomenon in nature, presents a compelling and potentially transformative concept for quantum algorithm design. This paper explores the application of this principle to optimize quantum circuit construction, focusing on the development of novel algorithms that harness repeating patterns at different scales. We propose a new approach predicated on identifying and exploiting fractal self-similarity within quantum circuits, resulting in enhanced computational performance and novel algorithmic capabilities. This work investigates the mathematical foundations of fractal self-similarity and demonstrates its practical implementation within a specific quantum algorithm framework. The paper will outline the core mechanism, detailing the process of defining a 'Fractal Scale' and utilizing iterative algorithms to exploit self-similarity. The ultimate goal is to leverage fractal self-similarity to unlock new possibilities in quantum computing, pushing the boundaries of what's currently achievable.

title: Core Claim: Design a self-adaptive graph neural network that dynamically adjusts graph structure based on noise and uncertainty, thereby enhancing the performance of graph neural networks.
abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for various machine learning tasks involving graph-structured data. However, traditional GNN architectures often struggle with noisy and uncertain graph environments, limiting their performance. This paper proposes a novel self-adaptive graph neural network that dynamically adjusts graph structure to mitigate these challenges. We introduce a novel "self-adaptive adjustment" mechanism, allowing the network to dynamically adjust the graph structure in response to noise and uncertainty. This mechanism is implemented using a combination of techniques including adaptive edge weighting and structural pruning. The results demonstrate that our self-adaptive GNN significantly outperforms existing approaches in scenarios characterized by high noise and uncertainty. This work contributes to the development of more robust and accurate GNNs suitable for a wider range of real-world applications.

The core mechanism centers around a self-regulating spin evolution driven by external stimuli, offering a pathway towards more robust and controllable quantum algorithms. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through theoretical analysis and preliminary experimental validation on a simplified quantum circuit. The results highlight the potential for significant improvements in both computational throughput and error mitigation within quantum computations.

title: Quantum Topology Geometry Geometric Analysis
abstract: Quantum topology, a burgeoning field of theoretical physics, explores the intersection of quantum mechanics and geometry, aiming to uncover fundamental geometric properties of space through quantum phenomena. This paper investigates the potential of quantum topology as a framework for analyzing geometric geometry, proposing a novel quantum computing approach to generate high-accuracy geometric representations. We outline the core claims, mechanisms, and potential impact of this approach, highlighting its promise to overcome limitations of traditional geometric analysis and offer a paradigm shift in geometric representation. The research explores the inherent geometric challenges posed by quantum mechanics and how these challenges can be addressed with quantum calculations.

title: Title: Adaptive Metric Learning for Sparse Data Clustering
abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive metric learning method designed specifically for sparse data clustering. Traditional metric learning algorithms often assume a uniform data distribution, which can be problematic when dealing with sparse datasets. This research proposes a novel approach that dynamically adjusts the metric learning algorithm based on the local data distribution, leading to improved accuracy and robustness in clustering scenarios. The core mechanism involves utilizing a self-adaptive distance metric that continuously evolves to better represent the data's characteristics. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through a series of experiments on diverse sparse datasets, showcasing its ability to effectively cluster data points while maintaining high accuracy. The method's adaptability addresses a critical limitation of existing techniques, enabling more effective clustering for real-world sparse data applications.

title: Scalable Edge-Based Multilingual Speech Processing for Secure Communication Environments
abstract: This paper presents a scalable edge-based multilingual speech processing system designed for secure communication environments with limited or intermittent network access. The proposed architecture integrates speech enhancement, language identification, streaming automatic speech recognition, confidence-aware re-ranking, and secure local output delivery within a unified on-premise framework. Experimental evaluation was conducted using a multilingual corpus containing clean speech, command phrases, and degraded radio-channel recordings in Kazakh, Russian, English, and Turkish. Results of the experiments indicate that practical deployment performance depends not only on recognition accuracy, but also on latency stability, thermal resilience, queue management, and robustness to mixed-language noisy speech.

title: Robust vision transformer adaptation for UAV imagery
abstract: , a structured distributional shift that can render an otherwise capable model dangerously unreliable in the field. Retraining or conventional domain adaptation is not a realistic option under the latency, compute, and annotation constraints of active disaster response. This work presents a comprehensive empirical evaluation of lightweight label-free test-time adaptation (TTA) methods for improving the robustness of ViTs under such deployment conditions, systematically comparing consistency-based self-supervision (MEMO) and entropy minimization (TENT) across datasets with varying classification complexity. Consistent with existing lightweight TTA approaches, only the LayerNorm affine parameters are adapted during inference, while the backbone and attention weights remain frozen. On the UAV-TEBDE post-earthquake dataset, accuracy rises from 73.47% under severe drift (severity 0.3) to 89.18% using MEMO, corresponding to a recovery of 15.71 percentage points over the drifted baseline, without using any ground-truth labels or performing any retraining. On UAV-TEBDE, MEMO also achieved higher recovery than the SAR baseline evaluated in this study. Additional evaluation on AID (30-class aerial scene classification) and UC Merced (21-class land-use classification) shows consistent drift-induced degradation and adaptation-driven recovery across datasets of varying complexity. The cross-dataset evaluation further reveals that the relative effectiveness of lightweight TTA methods depends on the classification-space dimensionality. TENT-based entropy minimization outperforms consistency-based MEMO when the class count is large, while MEMO is the stronger choice in low-class settings. This interaction between method design and classification-space dimensionality has direct consequences for choosing TTA strategies in operational disaster assessment pipelines. Feature-space PCA analysis confirms that LayerNorm-only updates geometrically recalibrate internal representations, rather than simply correcting the model's output logits.

title: Sentiment Analysis on Social Media Using BERT Model
abstract: The capacity to classify social media messages automatically regarding sentiment is increasingly crucial to understanding opinions of people. Current research advances prior sentiment detection investigations by revisiting performance of sentiment classification as per precision on social network datasets by utilizing BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) model. BERT model is utilized for improving sentiment classification performance on T4SA dataset in ongoing research and build on earlier unsupervised methods which have utilized manually constructed lexicons to detect extreme sentiments. Such findings display BERT poses potential to detect extreme emotions and improve classification performance significantly compared with past approaches while trained utilizing sufficient extreme sentiments dataset. Current investigation exposes probabilities of BERT for improving classification accuracy of social media sentiment detection, as part of advances in sentiment analysis. BERT‘s bidirectional encoding allows for accurate sentiment recognition by efficiently comprehending intricate verbal structures. The outcomes demonstrate BERT is a useful technique to examine public opinion, brand perception, and online discourse since it can distinguish subtle emotions in social media writing. Research concludes that BERT is an effective tool for sentiment analysis in social media because of its sophisticated contextual awareness and bidirectional encoding abilities.

title: A survey of world models for physical AI with uncertainty representation and control
abstract: Abstract Physical AI systems must reason about real-world dynamics in order to perceive, predict, and act safely under partial observability and uncertainty. World models–learned predictive representations of environment dynamics and action consequences–have emerged as a unifying framework for integrating perception, prediction, planning, and control in embodied agents. This survey provides a comprehensive and technically grounded review of learning-based world models for Physical AI, with particular emphasis on closed-loop decision-making. We organize existing approaches along six compositional design dimensions: state abstraction, temporal dynamics, uncertainty source and treatment, structural prior, observation modality, and decision coupling. Beyond this design-oriented taxonomy, we analyze how world models interact with optimization–highlighting compounding error, planner exploitation, rollout horizon management, and uncertainty calibration as central design tensions. We further examine evaluation methodologies, benchmark ecosystems, and sim-to-real transfer challenges, and synthesize open problems in long-horizon consistency, physical constraint enforcement, data efficiency, and safety. By clarifying recurring trade-offs across robotics and model-based reinforcement learning, this survey outlines principled directions for building reliable and scalable Physical AI systems.

title: Non-abelian quantum cellular automata: $1{+}1$-dimensional $SU(2)$ Yang--Mills with fermions
abstract: This work provides a digital quantum simulation scheme for $1{+}1$-dimensional $SU(2)$ Yang--Mills theory with Dirac fermions. It takes the form of a quantum circuit, infinitely repeating across space and time with $Δ_t=Δ_x=\varepsilon$, whose wires follow lightlike propagation. The construction mirrors the logic of the standard quantum field theory approach, transposed to the discrete setting. Namely, we start from the Dirac quantum walk, restore $SU(2)$ gauge symmetry by introducing the gauge field, lift the walk to a multi-particle QCA while preserving fermionic anticommutation, and equip the gauge field with its own dynamics. Rather than relying on Clebsch--Gordan decompositions, we use the pointwise-product structure of gauge-link updates, which yields self-contained proofs of unitarity and gauge covariance in quantum-computing notation. The construction provides an explicit algorithmic formulation of the theory, whose continuum limit we discuss.

title: RobustSeiz: An Open-Source Framework for Benchmarking the Robustness of EEG Seizure Detection Models
abstract: Despite strong performance on held-out electroencephalography (EEG) data, seizure detectors may fail under real-world acquisition variability, artifacts, and adversarial inputs. We introduce RobustSeiz, an open-source, model-agnostic framework that provides a standardized, reproducible protocol for stress-testing and comparing seizure detectors under controlled, clinically motivated distribution shifts before deployment. We standardize four public scalp-EEG corpora (CHB-MIT, TUSZ, Siena, and SeizeIT1) into BIDS-EEG trees and evaluate subject-independent detectors on held-out splits. Environment, noise, and adversarial transforms are swept over predefined hyperparameter grids. Each run reports sample- and event-level sensitivity, precision, F1, false positives per 24 h, Lead and Lag onset timing, and Monte Carlo dropout predictive agreement. RobustSeiz includes a Dockerized GPU pipeline, experiment registry, and full-evaluation and research-subset modes. We demonstrate the framework with a contemporary seizure detector on TUSZ across the complete implemented shift grid; an AWGN analysis illustrates how perturbation severity changes detection quality, onset timing, and predictive agreement. RobustSeiz provides a shared benchmarking standard for evaluating seizure-detector robustness under realistic clinical stressors, extending pre-deployment assessment beyond clean-data accuracy.

title: Observation-Conditioned Latent Energy Priors for Sparse Implicit Neural Shape Completion
abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) can model continuous 3D shapes with a shared coordinate decoder and per-instance latent codes. At test time, autodecoder-style models commonly freeze the decoder and optimize a new latent code from sparse off-grid SDF samples. When these samples underconstrain inference, the latent can drift toward regions that fit the observations but decode implausible unobserved geometry. We propose a post-hoc observation-conditioned latent energy prior for frozen INR decoders. The energy scores standardized latents conditioned on a permutation-invariant encoding of the sparse observation set and is used as a residual expert alongside an L2 latent prior selected on validation data. We evaluate on a controlled cell-nucleus SDF dataset and a public MedShapeNet-derived SDF completion dataset. The proposed L2 objective augmented with conditional energy improves consistently over a validation-selected L2 baseline in the sparsest cell-nucleus regimes and, on MedShapeNet, outperforms both L2 and a six-component GMM latent-density prior across all reported readouts. A shuffled-context ablation is consistently weaker than matched context, supporting an observation-specific contribution. These results suggest that lightweight conditional energies can make pretrained INR decoders more observation-aware without retraining.

title: Adaptive-Preprocessing-Enhanced YOLOX-L For Breast Cancer Mass Detection in Contrast-Enhanced Spectral Mammography
abstract: Breast cancer detection using contrast-enhanced spectral mammography (CESM) is still a challenging task, especially when lesions are subtle, low in contrast, or located within dense breast tissue. In this paper, an automated breast mass localization pipeline was developed using the YOLOX-L object detection framework. The proposed pipeline applies a piecewise adaptive contrast enhancement method before the detection stage. This method depends on dynamic thresholding to improve the visibility of lesion regions while preserving the surrounding anatomical structures. The proposed method was evaluated using the public CDD-CESM dataset. The enhanced YOLOX-L model achieved a mAP@0.50:0.95 of 0.703, while the unenhanced baseline achieved 0.186 under the same evaluation setting. Furthermore, additional experiments showed that the proposed enhancement method performed better than histogram equalization and CLAHE when using the same patient-level split, training configuration, and evaluation protocol. The pipeline also achieved near-real-time inference under the tested computational environment. Hence, the proposed system may be useful as an assistive tool for CESM breast mass detection. However, further external and prospective validation is still required before clinical use.

title: Quantum Entanglement and Non-Linear Time Expansion Algorithm
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, offers a potential pathway to revolutionize computation. This paper explores the application of entanglement to a novel algorithm, termed "Non-Linear Time Expansion Algorithm" (NLTEA), designed to exploit the non-linear properties of entangled states to achieve significant computational speedups. The core mechanism of NLTEA involves carefully manipulating entangled states to induce a temporal distortion, demonstrating a unique approach to time-expanding computation. We present a theoretical framework and preliminary results demonstrating the algorithm's potential for enhanced computational efficiency. The goal is to unlock new possibilities within quantum computing, moving beyond traditional algorithmic optimizations.

title: Dynamic Quantum Resource Allocation Algorithm
abstract: This paper presents a novel dynamic quantum resource allocation algorithm designed to optimize quantum computing efficiency. The core claim is that static quantum resource allocation is insufficient for diverse quantum computing tasks. The proposed mechanism dynamically adjusts resource allocation based on task characteristics and current state, addressing this limitation. The algorithm incorporates a feedback loop analyzing task progress and resource utilization to refine the allocation strategy in real-time. This approach aims to mitigate the challenges of resource contention and maximize the utilization of available quantum resources, leading to improved performance across a range of quantum computing applications. The algorithm's effectiveness is evaluated through theoretical analysis and conceptual design, laying the groundwork for future experimental validation. The key innovation lies in its adaptability, contrasting with existing methods that typically employ fixed resource assignments.

title: 基于动态的机器学习的自适应损失函数
abstract: This paper introduces a novel loss function framework based on dynamic machine learning, specifically designed to enhance model performance through adaptive weight adjustment. Traditional loss functions typically employ fixed parameters, restricting the model's ability to capture complex relationships within the data. Our approach utilizes a dynamic loss function that dynamically adjusts the weighting of different components during training, effectively learning more optimal and efficient loss functions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through a series of experiments on a diverse dataset, showcasing significant improvements in model accuracy and generalization ability compared to baseline models. The core mechanism involves an iterative process of analyzing feature dependencies and dynamically modifying the loss function's parameters, promoting a more flexible and robust learning process.

title: Based on Quantum Entanglement: Non-Local Information Transfer
abstract: This paper explores the potential of utilizing quantum entanglement for non-local information transfer, a concept that fundamentally challenges the limitations imposed by classical physics and conventional communication methods. The core claim presented is the possibility of leveraging entanglement's non-locality to achieve information transfer exceeding the speed of light, paving the way for distributed computing architectures with enhanced capabilities. This work details a proposed mechanism for constructing a quantum entanglement network, focusing on manipulating and measuring entangled states to facilitate information transmission. The design incorporates techniques for encoding and decoding information through entanglement superposition and interference. While acknowledging current limitations such as quantum decoherence, this research highlights the significant, albeit challenging, potential of non-local information transfer via entanglement. The theoretical framework presented aims to stimulate further investigation into this revolutionary approach to communication and computation. ---

title: Predictive Coding with Hierarchical Latent Representations and Temporal Recurrence
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to predictive coding that addresses the limitations of traditional methods in modeling complex temporal dependencies and hierarchical structures. The core idea is to integrate hierarchical latent representations with temporal recurrence mechanisms within a predictive coding framework. This combination allows the network to learn and predict patterns that span multiple temporal scales, resulting in a more robust and flexible model. The proposed system utilizes a hierarchical structure to represent information at different levels of abstraction, while temporal recurrence enables the network to capture and predict temporal dependencies effectively. This approach moves beyond the limitations of standard predictive coding, offering a more sophisticated solution for modeling dynamic systems and temporal data. The key innovation lies in the synergistic interaction between these three components, enabling the network to learn richer and more accurate predictive models. Mathematical formulations are presented to formally describe the architecture and dynamics of the system.

title: Adaptive Quantum Circuit Compilation for Hardware-Aware Optimization
abstract: Quantum circuit compilation is a critical step in realizing quantum algorithms on real quantum hardware. Traditional compilation methods often employ static optimization strategies, neglecting the unique constraints and characteristics of the target quantum device. This paper introduces a novel adaptive quantum circuit compilation framework designed to dynamically adjust circuit designs based on hardware-specific information, aiming to minimize gate count and, consequently, error rates. The core of the framework lies in integrating a hardware simulator directly within the compilation process. This allows the compiler to evaluate the performance of various circuit designs—considering factors like qubit connectivity, gate fidelity, and decoherence models—before committing to a final layout. The proposed approach represents a shift from static to adaptive optimization, providing a more nuanced and effective strategy for translating quantum algorithms into executable code on diverse quantum hardware platforms. This research demonstrates a significant potential improvement in quantum circuit efficiency and fidelity, addressing a key bottleneck in the advancement of quantum computing.

title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Intrinsic Motivation and Hierarchical Control
abstract: This paper investigates the challenges of applying standard multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) to complex, dynamic environments. The core problem lies in the difficulty agents face when navigating environments with high dimensionality, sparse rewards, and intricate interactions. We propose a novel framework that addresses this issue by integrating intrinsic motivation with hierarchical reinforcement learning within a multi-agent system. This approach enables agents to proactively explore and learn, mitigating the limitations of purely extrinsic reward-based learning. Specifically, we introduce a hierarchical control structure where higher-level agents set strategic goals, while lower-level agents execute these goals using intrinsic motivation to drive exploration and adapt to the environment. The key equation demonstrating the overall reward function is: R = R_ext + λ * R_int, where R_ext is the extrinsic reward, R_int is the intrinsic reward, and λ is a weighting factor. Furthermore, the exploration bonus is defined as b_e(s, a) = α * log(π(s, a)) , where α is the exploration parameter, and π(s, a) is the probability distribution over actions in state s. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework through a theoretical analysis and illustrate its potential with a simplified example. This work contributes to the field of MARL by offering a more robust and efficient learning strategy for complex environments.

title: Quantum Neural Networks: Adaptive Learning Strategies
abstract: Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) represent a promising paradigm shift in machine learning, leveraging the unique properties of quantum mechanics to potentially surpass classical neural networks. This paper explores the application of QNNs to adaptive learning, proposing a novel self-adaptive learning strategy that dynamically adjusts network parameters and structural configurations based on the network's evolving state. We present a framework centered around quantum entanglement and superposition, enabling a continuous, nuanced adjustment of the learning process. The core mechanism focuses on leveraging the inherent quantum properties to optimize learning efficiency. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through simulations and preliminary experiments, illustrating a significant improvement in learning speed and robustness compared to traditional approaches. The resulting QNN demonstrates a key advantage: a more flexible and adaptable learning process, offering a pathway towards truly intelligent and efficient learning.

title: Quantum Random Number Generator Based on Quantum Mechanical Principles
abstract: This paper presents the design and theoretical framework for a quantum random number generator (QRNG) rooted in the principles of quantum mechanics. The core innovation lies in leveraging the inherent randomness associated with quantum measurement, specifically the uncertainty principle, to generate truly random numbers, a significant departure from the limitations of classical random number generators. The proposed system utilizes a measurement process involving a quantum system, such as a photon polarization or a quantum bit, to produce a sequence of random bits. The generated bits are then processed to eliminate bias and ensure high uniformity. The theoretical analysis focuses on quantifying the randomness inherent in the measurement process and demonstrating the potential for generating high-quality random numbers. This work addresses the growing demand for secure communication, cryptography, and simulation applications that require truly random numbers, offering a fundamentally different approach compared to traditional methods.

title: Title: Bayesian Geometric Chaos with Adaptive Smoothing
abstract: This paper investigates the challenges of analyzing and predicting chaotic systems, particularly those exhibiting inherent uncertainty. Traditional Bayesian methods often struggle to effectively model and quantify this uncertainty, leading to inaccurate predictions. We introduce a novel Bayesian geometric chaos framework centered around an adaptive smoothing algorithm. This framework leverages Bayesian inference to estimate the system's sensitivity to initial conditions while dynamically adjusting the uncertainty estimates based on observed behavior. The core mechanism involves integrating a curvature-aware Bayesian approach that continuously refines the model's representation of the system's dynamics, resulting in improved predictive accuracy and a more robust understanding of chaotic behavior. The proposed method offers a significant advancement over existing techniques, particularly in handling the inherent uncertainty within complex, nonlinear dynamical systems.

This work leverages the inherent properties of geometric space data – its geometric structure and inherent relationships – to implement an iterative refinement process that automatically adjusts the clustering standard. We propose a novel approach that iteratively adjusts the distance metric and cluster threshold based on the data's geometry, resulting in more meaningful and robust clusters. The algorithm's performance is evaluated using a benchmark dataset, demonstrating improved clustering accuracy and a reduction in variance compared to existing methods.

title: Quantum Information Entropy Dynamics – A Dynamic Calculation Based on Quantum State Adaptation
abstract: Quantum information entropy is a fundamental property of quantum systems, representing the uncertainty associated with the system's state. Efficiently compressing and transmitting quantum information requires minimizing the entropy, while simultaneously maximizing the fidelity of the transmitted states. This paper proposes a novel dynamic calculation method for quantum information entropy, leveraging the inherent adaptability of quantum states to achieve enhanced compression and transmission efficiency, particularly in the context of quantum information transfer. The core mechanism centers around utilizing quantum state adaptation to dynamically adjust the system's state, thereby minimizing the entropy without compromising fidelity. This approach offers a fundamentally different pathway to data management compared to traditional methods, potentially revolutionizing quantum communication protocols.

title: Title: Adaptive Topology for Signal Processing in High Dimensional Spaces
abstract: This paper investigates the application of adaptive topology in signal processing, specifically focusing on optimizing performance within high-dimensional spaces. Traditional signal processing algorithms often struggle with dimensionality, leading to computational bottlenecks and suboptimal results. This work proposes a novel topology – the "Adaptive Topology" – that dynamically adjusts its structure to the dimensionality of the input data, enhancing efficiency through a combination of dimensionality reduction and sparse connectivity. The core mechanism involves a sophisticated "dimensionality reduction" technique, coupled with a carefully designed sparse connectivity scheme. The resulting topology offers a promising approach to mitigate the challenges associated with high-dimensional data, providing potential improvements in signal processing efficiency and robustness. The study explores the effectiveness of this approach through simulations and preliminary analysis, demonstrating its capacity to handle complex signal patterns effectively.

This work introduces a method that automatically adjusts network structure by dynamically adjusting layer and neuron counts, leading to improved model performance. title: Quantum State Transfer for Parallel Computation
abstract: Quantum state transfer is a crucial element in quantum computing, representing the fundamental process of moving quantum states between processors. Current limitations in quantum computation are largely driven by the inherent fragility of quantum states, making efficient transfer a significant bottleneck. This paper proposes a novel protocol for quantum state transfer centered around entanglement, designed to drastically accelerate complex calculations by minimizing entanglement loss and maximizing computational throughput. We delve into the challenges of maintaining entanglement coherence during transfer and introduce a mechanism that strategically leverages entanglement to achieve this goal. The core claim is that this protocol, utilizing a carefully designed entanglement network, will significantly improve the performance of parallel computations, offering a practical pathway to overcome the limitations imposed by the qubit count.

title: Calcyon: An AI-Based Chatbot Framework for Calculus Learning to Support Computational Thinking Skill and Self-Regulated Learning
abstract: Abstract* Background The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into mathematics education has advanced rapidly, yet limited attention has been given to systematic AI based chatbot frameworks that integrate computational thinking (CT) and self regulated learning (SRL) scaffolding within university calculus. This study developed and validated Calcyon, an AI based chatbot framework designed to support differential calculus learning through coordinated CT and SRL scaffolding. Methods A Research and Development approach guided by the ADDIE model was employed. Expert validation (n = 3) was conducted across five quality dimensions using Aiken's V formula. A student pilot readability and feasibility test (n = 11) assessed practical usability across six dimensions. A design and development research approach guided by the ADDIE model was employed. Three experts evaluated the framework across five quality dimensions using a four point rating scale, with content validity assessed using Aiken's V. A formative pilot involving 11 undergraduate calculus students evaluated readability and feasibility across six dimensions. Results Expert validation indicated that Calcyon demonstrated strong validity across the evaluated content, instructional, technical, linguistic, and media design dimensions. Most validation items met the predefined validity criterion, while a small number were refined based on expert feedback. The student pilot further indicated good readability and feasibility, with responses showing consistently positive evaluations of the prototype. Conclusions Calcyon provides an empirically validated instructional design framework that combines AI mediated interaction with explicit CT and SRL scaffolding for university calculus. The findings support the framework's expert rated validity and preliminary readability and feasibility. Further experimental research is required to determine its effectiveness in improving CT, SRL, and calculus learning outcomes.

title: Restricting Trainable Lie-Algebra Growth in Equivariant Quantum Networks via Hierarchical Ancilla-Controlled Subspace Projections
abstract: Equivariant quantum networks encode symmetry as an inductive bias, which can improve generalization and may also favor optimization convergence. Equivariance alone, however, does not constrain the noncommuting closure of trainable generators, and this closure can still grow rapidly in symmetry-preserving variational circuits. We introduce a hierarchical ancilla-controlled architecture that addresses this Lie-algebra-growth mechanism. Commuting invariant-sector projectors on the data register select parameterized operations on a shared ancilla register, where the noncommuting trainable dynamics is confined. The trainable circuit decomposes into compatible joint sectors, giving a sector-probability-weighted ancilla response and an explicit view of parameter sharing across hierarchical paths. For an ancilla dimension $d_A=2^m$ and $K_\ell$ retained layer-wise control modes, we prove the group-independent bound $\dim(\mathfrak g)\le (d_A^2-1)\prod_{\ell=1}^{L}(K_\ell+1)$. The bound is polynomial in the number of data qubits when $m$ and $K_\ell$ remain constant along a logarithmic-depth hierarchy. Particle-number and parity projectors illustrate the general construction, while a fixed Clebsch--Gordan coupling tree supplies a concrete $SU(2)$ realization with rotation-invariant scalar outputs. Finite-size state-vector simulations exhibit slower gradient-variance decay and larger initialization gradients than generic and conventional rotationally equivariant circuits over the studied system sizes. The same realization fits sparse rotation-invariant classification tasks and geometry-dependent Heisenberg ground-state energies. These results support restricted trainable Lie-algebra growth as a structural strategy for initialization trainability in the regimes considered here.

title: Abstract-LoRA: Unlocking Single-Image Style Transfer through Targeted U-Net Block Training
abstract: Diffusion models represent one of the most advanced paradigms in generative modeling. Leveraging their development, a growing number of style transfer methods based on diffusion models have been proposed. However, among these methods, multi-image style transfer approaches that require at least five to ten style examples tend to achieve more satisfactory results. Single-image methods, by contrast, often struggle with either insufficient content preservation or inadequate style fidelity. This greatly limits style extraction from scarce artworks and undermines their artistic value. To address this, we propose Abstract-LoRA, a method that pushes the boundaries of single-image style transfer through lightweight LoRA training on specific U-Net blocks in diffusion models. Specifically, our work is inspired by B-LoRA, a style transfer method that achieves basic style-content disentanglement by training specific U-Net blocks. However, it suffers from a critical limitation: the inability to capture complex backgrounds. Building upon B-LoRA, our method conducts a more refined analysis of U-Net blocks, employing additional U-Net blocks and clustering-based abstraction of style images to better disentangle and balance style and content. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed method not only generates visually more harmonious and satisfying artistic images but also quantitatively improves the preservation of both style and content in the final outputs.

title: Proof-of-principle long-distance Sagnac twin-field quantum key distribution network
abstract: Twin-field (TF) quantum key distribution (QKD) offers a promising approach to long-distance QKD networks due to its superior performance over large channel losses. Due to specialized hardware requirements, nearly all long-distance TFQKD demonstrations have only two users exchanging keys, rather than a network with three or more users. In this work, we experimentally demonstrate a proof-of-principle three-user-pair Sagnac TFQKD network spanning 127-km using single-photon avalanche detectors without any active phase stabilization or postcompensation. We implement efficient procedures for maintaining polarization stability and circumventing Rayleigh backscattering noise to achieve a stable Sagnac interference visibility of $93\pm1$% over one hour. A secure key rate of $1.398\times10^{-5}$ bits per pulse is achieved over an asymmetric communication channel with 102-km fiber and 45-dB overall loss. To our knowledge, this is the first TFQKD network without active phase stabilization or postcompensation achieved over long fibers. Our results represent a highly practical and cost-effective approach to long-distance QKD networks.

title: Optimización de hiperparámetros en redes perceptrón multicapa tradicionales mediante búsqueda exploratoria de códigos variables
abstract: The problem of hyperparameter optimization in multilayer perceptron neural networks for non-linear continuous regression tasks was addressed. A heuristic method termed Exploratory Search at the Extreme of a Variable Code Function, derived from the Variable Integration Method, was proposed. The optimization problem was formulated using a Chebyshev distance scalarization that simultaneously balances predictive accuracy (R²) and generalization across training, validation, and test sets. The method was evaluated on five UCI regression datasets. Comparisons against Random Search and Bayesian Optimization demonstrated statistically significant improvements in mean squared error versus Bayesian Optimization (p = 0.031), with low variability across independent runs. Keywords: Artificial neural networks, multi-objective optimization, heuristics, non-linear regression, hyperparameter optimization

title: Quantum Bayesian Networks with Dynamic Kernel Calibration
abstract: Quantum Bayesian Networks (QBNs) offer a promising framework for probabilistic reasoning, particularly in complex systems with inherent uncertainty. Traditional QBNs rely on fixed, static kernels, which can struggle to effectively handle noisy data and evolving patterns. This paper introduces a novel approach to QBN modeling that incorporates a dynamic kernel calibration mechanism, enabling the network to adapt to observed uncertainty and improve predictive accuracy. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through simulations and preliminary experiments, showcasing its ability to outperform existing methods in scenarios with high noise levels and complex dependencies.

title: 基于自适应的强化学习的神经网络模型设计
abstract: This paper introduces a novel neural network architecture based on adaptive reinforcement learning (ARL) to enhance reinforcement learning performance. Traditional reinforcement learning models often struggle with complex data and model variations due to their static nature. Our proposed algorithm dynamically adjusts network structure and learning rates through a learned parameterization, enabling the model to adapt more effectively to changing environments. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through extensive experiments on several benchmark reinforcement learning tasks, showcasing significant improvements in sample efficiency and convergence speed. The core mechanism involves a self-tuning parameterization that learns optimal network parameters based on the observed reward signal.

title: Non-Linear Stability Theory: A Quantum Computing Simulation Framework
abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for simulating non-linear stability theory using quantum computing. Traditional methods rely on classical computational techniques, often limiting the accuracy and scalability of simulations. This work leverages quantum computing's unique properties, specifically superposition and entanglement, to provide a fundamentally different approach to stability analysis and prediction. We propose a quantum simulation algorithm designed to accurately model complex non-linear systems, offering enhanced precision and control over stability characteristics. The core mechanism involves employing quantum algorithms to represent and manipulate the system's dynamics, while simultaneously utilizing quantum superposition to efficiently explore the solution space. This research aims to advance the field of stability theory by providing a powerful and efficient simulation tool with potential implications for various engineering and scientific disciplines.

title: Distributed Causal Inference using Federated Learning and Bayesian Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for distributed causal inference by integrating federated learning with Bayesian networks. Traditional causal inference methods often require centralized data access, posing significant privacy concerns and logistical challenges, particularly in scenarios involving sensitive data distributed across multiple entities. Our approach addresses this limitation by enabling each participating entity to simultaneously learn causal relationships within its local data using Bayesian networks. These locally learned models are then aggregated to construct a global causal model, mitigating the need for centralized data sharing. We introduce a specific federated learning architecture tailored for causal discovery, incorporating techniques to address confounding and selection bias. The core of the method lies in the iterative refinement of Bayesian network structures through distributed learning, followed by weighted averaging of the learned parameters. We demonstrate the potential of this method through a theoretical analysis, outlining its advantages in terms of privacy preservation, scalability, and robustness. The resulting global causal model provides insights into the underlying causal relationships while respecting data locality. evidence.title: Distributed Causal Inference using Federated Learning and Bayesian Networks
evidence.abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for distributed causal inference by integrating federated learning with Bayesian networks. Traditional causal inference methods often require centralized data access, posing significant privacy concerns and logistical challenges, particularly in scenarios involving sensitive data distributed across multiple entities. Our approach addresses this limitation by enabling each participating entity to simultaneously learn causal relationships within its local data using Bayesian networks. These locally learned models are then aggregated to construct a global causal model, mitigating the need for centralized data sharing. We introduce a specific federated learning architecture tailored for causal discovery, incorporating techniques to address confounding and selection bias. The core of the method lies in the iterative refinement of Bayesian network structures through distributed learning, followed by weighted averaging of the learned parameters. We demonstrate the potential of this method through a theoretical analysis, outlining its advantages in terms of privacy preservation, scalability, and robustness. The resulting global causal model provides insights into the underlying causal relationships while respecting data locality. This approach offers a viable pathway for causal inference in distributed, privacy-sensitive environments.

title: Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning with Intrinsic Motivation and Cognitive Maps
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to reinforcement learning (RL) that integrates hierarchical control, cognitive mapping, and intrinsic motivation. The core idea is to create an agent capable of building a detailed understanding of its environment while simultaneously driving its own exploration. The proposed architecture utilizes a hierarchical structure, separating planning and execution. The planner leverages a learned cognitive map – a spatial representation of the environment – to generate high-level goals. The executor then translates these goals into low-level actions, guided by intrinsic rewards that are dynamically adjusted based on novelty and surprise. The learning process is therefore driven not only by external rewards but also by the agent's own curiosity and desire to discover new aspects of the environment. This combination offers a potential pathway to overcoming the limitations of traditional RL in complex, sparse-reward environments, leading to more efficient and robust learning. The key contribution lies in the synergistic interaction between these three components, leading to a more adaptive and intelligent agent.

title: Self-Correcting Neural Networks via Predictive Coding with Entropy Regularization
abstract: Neural networks, despite their successes in various domains, are susceptible to accumulating errors during the training process. This often leads to suboptimal performance and instability. This paper proposes a novel self-correcting framework for neural networks that addresses this issue by integrating predictive coding and entropy regularization. The core idea is to have the network predict its own outputs. The prediction error, or residual, is then propagated backward through the network, effectively correcting the network's internal state. Simultaneously, entropy regularization is applied to encourage the learning of robust and resilient representations, minimizing the network's sensitivity to noise and outliers. We demonstrate that this combined approach significantly improves training stability and often leads to better performance compared to standard training methods. The theoretical underpinnings of this approach are presented, and we outline the key components of the architecture and training procedure. The effectiveness of this framework is illustrated through a conceptual analysis and a discussion of potential implementation details.

title: Adaptive Data Augmentation Based on Information Entropy
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to data augmentation that leverages the information entropy of individual features within a dataset. The core idea is to analyze the entropy distribution of these features and dynamically adjust the augmentation strategy based on the resulting entropy values. Traditional data augmentation techniques often employ global, uniform methods, which can introduce unwanted noise or distort the underlying data distribution, negatively impacting model performance. Our method offers a more intelligent and adaptive approach, focusing on areas of high entropy – where more aggressive augmentation is warranted – and low entropy – where subtle adjustments are sufficient. We introduce a model to estimate feature entropy and utilize this estimation to guide the augmentation process. This approach promises improved data augmentation effectiveness and potentially enhanced model accuracy.

title: High-Order Geometry Quantum Simulation
abstract: This paper explores the potential of high-order geometry to provide a novel approach to quantum simulation, focusing on the study of quantum systems exhibiting high-order geometric structures. We propose a framework that leverages the inherent properties of high-order geometry to enhance the accuracy and interpretability of quantum simulations. The core mechanism involves constructing a quantum system based on high-order geometric principles, enabling a deeper understanding of the system's behavior through quantum computation. This work introduces a new methodology for investigating complex quantum phenomena and offers a potential pathway towards more sophisticated simulations. The paper concludes with a discussion of the challenges and future directions in this field.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Geometric Optimization of Fluid Dynamics
abstract: Quantum-enhanced geometric optimization of fluid dynamics aims to address limitations in classical simulations by introducing quantum algorithms to refine fluid flow predictions. This research explores the application of quantum annealing and VQE to optimize fluid dynamics, specifically focusing on enhancing stability and flow rate. The core mechanism involves leveraging geometric concepts – particularly the shape and topology of fluid domains – to guide quantum optimization, ultimately leading to improved simulation accuracy and computational efficiency. The novelty lies in the integration of quantum mechanics with geometric principles, a previously unexplored avenue for fluid dynamics modeling. This paper details the theoretical framework, algorithm design, and preliminary results demonstrating the potential of this approach.

title: Algorithmic Self-Assembly of Quantum Circuits
abstract: This paper explores the potential for algorithmic self-assembly to revolutionize quantum circuit design. Traditionally, quantum circuit design is a highly manual and often inefficient process, heavily reliant on expert intuition and trial-and-error. We propose a novel approach where a quantum circuit is treated as a self-assembling system, governed by an evolutionary algorithm. This algorithm iteratively refines circuit topology and gate parameters to meet pre-specified performance criteria – such as fidelity, circuit depth, and gate count. The core claim is that by mimicking the self-assembly behavior observed in biological systems, we can automate the creation of optimized quantum circuits. This work formalizes this process, outlining a genetic algorithm that drives the automated design. The system's ability to explore a vast design space and adapt to complex performance requirements represents a significant advancement in the field, potentially unlocking the full capabilities of quantum computation. This paper details the algorithm's architecture, the optimization criteria, and the underlying mathematical framework, showcasing a viable path towards automated quantum circuit construction.

title: 基于高阶矩阵的动态隐马尔可夫过程 (DMM) 优化
abstract: The Dynamic Hidden Markov Model (DMM) is a powerful tool in machine learning, particularly in areas like probabilistic graphical models and natural language processing. However, training and optimizing DMM models can be computationally expensive and require careful parameter tuning. This paper introduces a novel algorithm, leveraging high-order matrix operations, to accelerate and refine the optimization process for DMMs. We propose a new method to dynamically adjust the parameters of the DMM, enhancing model accuracy and efficiency. This approach addresses the limitations of existing methods by providing a more robust and adaptable optimization strategy. The core mechanism involves the application of a custom matrix transformation to guide the parameter updates, resulting in significantly improved performance compared to traditional methods. We present experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of this algorithm on several DMM datasets, showcasing its ability to achieve higher accuracy and reduced training time.

title: Title: Dynamic Graph-Based Distributed Computing Adaptive Model Optimization
abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for distributed model optimization based on dynamic graphs. Traditional approaches often rely on static parameter settings and limited training data, hindering the ability to dynamically adjust model parameters to enhance efficiency and accuracy. Our proposed system leverages dynamic graph adjustments to automatically optimize model parameters, resulting in improved computational efficiency and predictive performance. The core mechanism centers around the utilization of dynamic graphs to dynamically adjust model parameters during the optimization process, fostering a more adaptive and effective optimization strategy. This work contributes to the advancement of distributed model optimization techniques by introducing a framework that dynamically responds to changes in model parameters and data, offering a significant improvement over existing methods. Core Claim: We propose a dynamic graph-based distributed computing framework for adaptive model optimization, dynamically adjusting model parameters to improve computational efficiency and accuracy, leveraging the benefits of dynamic graph adjustments. Core Mechanism: The core mechanism of this framework involves constructing a dynamic graph that represents the model parameters and their relationships. This dynamic graph is continuously updated and adjusted based on feedback from the model's performance during training. The framework utilizes a graph-based approach to efficiently model the model's state and dynamically adjust parameters to minimize error and optimize performance. This adaptive adjustment leverages the inherent properties of dynamic graphs to facilitate faster optimization and improved accuracy. Why It Is New: While existing distributed model optimization techniques often employ static parameter tuning or limited adaptive strategies, the current research focuses on a dynamically adjusting framework utilizing dynamic graphs. This approach addresses a key limitation in traditional methods, offering a more flexible and automated optimization process. The integration of dynamic graph adjustments introduces a novel mechanism for proactive model parameter optimization, potentially leading to substantial improvements in efficiency and accuracy compared to static approaches.

abstract: Quantum topology, a burgeoning field of physics, promises revolutionary advancements in computation and information processing. Within this landscape, Quantum Topology Language (QTTL) emerges as a novel framework for automating the creation of quantum algorithms and models, significantly accelerating the research and development process. This paper explores the concept of QTTL and its potential to streamline quantum computing initiatives. We detail the core mechanism behind QTTL, focusing on leveraging the unique properties of quantum topology to generate effective and adaptable quantum algorithms. The benefits of automated QTTL generation are discussed, including reduced development costs and accelerated innovation within the quantum computing community.

title: RI: Towards a Deeper Understanding of In-Context Learning
abstract: Language models have become central to computing, but our understanding of how they work internally has not kept pace with their deployment. This gap has critical implications for the broader use of models in society. When a model fails, gives inconsistent answers across different phrasings of the same prompt, or follows an instruction it should have declined, we typically cannot say exactly why. Work in mechanistic interpretability offers a potential alternative: model behaviors can often be traced to specific internal components and the information they exchange, and behaviors that can be traced can potentially be predicted, corrected, and controlled. This proposal argues that a key capability for which such understanding is needed, and where it is now within reach, is \emph{in-context learning} (ICL). Broadly, in-context learning is the ability of a model to learn at \emph{inference time} from the input it is given. This is in sharp contrast to the traditional model of machine learning as a process that occurs at training time. Understanding ICL is important for improving model capabilities because it can reveal the mechanisms that allow models to rapidly infer tasks, representations, and patterns from limited evidence at inference time. It is equally important for model safety, since contextual information can cause models to adopt unintended behaviors, override otherwise desirable tendencies, or generalize instructions in unexpected ways. Unfortunately, despite the considerable work done to date, a broad understanding of ICL is lacking. Despite extensive work, we do not yet have a general account of what information models extract from context, how that information is represented internally, or how it alters the computation that produces subsequent outputs. Accordingly, our proposed work will seek broad answers to a central question: What learning method does a pretrained language model actually perform on a particular prompt, where is that method implemented, and why does it choose that computation rather than another? To resolve this question, we identify three specific research questions whose answers would substantially advance our understanding of ICL. First: to clearly identify the phenomenon we seek to study, we must develop methods to distinguish task recognition from genuine task learning. Second: how is an in-context task represented, and how does that representation control downstream computation? That is, how are ICL tasks in general implemented in language models? Do tasks share reusable modules, and if so, which ones? Third: how is knowledge obtained at inference time unified with pretrained knowledge? Can we understand quantitatively and mechanistically how in-context evidence supporting a particular output is integrated with evidence present in model weights? Answering these three questions will be aided by the use of two new toolsets developed in our laboratory. First, attention mean-field analysis provides a strong null model for contextual processing by a model, enabling characterization of potential ICL at the level of individual prompts, tokens, and model components. Second, attention-causal circuit tracing enables precise identification of model components that are responsible for a computation such as an ICL instance. Our proposal describes the methods we will use to answer to our three questions, including how these tools can help unlock those answers, and the initial progress we have made that suggests that those answers may be attainable.

title: AI applications in physical retail: technologies, consumer interaction, and operational impact
abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in physical retail environments is transforming customer experiences and operational efficiency. While research on AI technologies such as chatbots, virtual assistants, computer vision, and machine learning has grown rapidly, it remains fragmented, often focusing on isolated technologies or single aspects of the retail experience. This study addresses this fragmentation by systematically synthesizing prior findings through a systematic literature review (SLR) of 50 peer-reviewed studies to develop a unified understanding of how AI transforms the in-store customer journey. AI applications were categorized along three dimensions: (A) AI technologies, (B) application areas, and (C) resulting impacts. The synthesis reveals that AI enhances customer engagement through personalized recommendations and interactive service tools while optimizing backend processes such as inventory management, pricing, and checkout automation. However, three key challenges persist: (1) AI’s limited emotional intelligence, (2) ethical concerns regarding data privacy and algorithmic transparency, and (3) scalability and integration constraints in physical retail settings. This research contributes to the existing literature by offering a conceptual framework for AI adoption in retail, synthesizing prior research across the pre-engagement, in-store experience, and post-purchase phases. It highlights the strategic tensions between customer engagement and operational goals, emphasizing the need for ethical governance and cross-functional AI integration. The study advances theoretical understanding and provides actionable insights for both academics and practitioners, outlining avenues for future research on AI-driven retail innovations.

This research contributes to the existing literature by offering a conceptual framework for AI adoption in retail, synthesizing prior research across the pre-engagement, in-store experience, and post-purchase phases. It highlights the strategic tensions between customer engagement and operational goals, emphasizing the need for ethical governance and cross-functional AI integration. The study advances theoretical understanding and provides actionable insights for both academics and practitioners, outlining avenues for future research on AI-driven retail innovations.

title: MetaStructAtlas: A Grounded 3D Vision-Language Dataset and Benchmark for Functional and Structural Reasoning in Whole-Body PET/CT
abstract: The joint interpretation of metabolic function and anatomical structure is essential for clinical diagnosis in whole-body PET/CT. Although recent advances in 3D medical vision-language models have demonstrated remarkable progress, current efforts are limited to regional CT imaging, leaving a critical void in comprehensive whole-body PET/CT analysis. In this work, we introduce MetaStructAtlas, a large-scale dataset for grounded whole-body PET/CT interpretation that synthesizes multimodal imaging with integrated anatomical, metabolic, and semantic annotations. MetaStructAtlas provides 490 co-registered 3D PET and CT volumes with 50,470 organ-level segmentation masks and grounded radiology reports. To facilitate interactive reasoning, we further developed MetaStructVQA, a standardized 3D grounded visual question-answering benchmark containing 100,565 QA pairs. This framework explicitly links diagnostic queries to visual evidence across modalities, encompassing anatomical, morphological, and metabolic characteristics. Finally, we evaluate state-of-the-art 3D medical VLMs on MetaStructVQA, establishing a robust foundation for multimodal representation learning and integrated whole-body reasoning in nuclear medicine.

title: Beyond Straightness: Non-Crossing Flow Matching via Quantile AlignTree Coupling
abstract: The performance of Flow Matching largely depends on the quality of the coupling between the source and target distributions. However, independent coupling often leads to path crossings and local velocity ambiguity, while OT-based couplings typically incur high construction costs. To address this challenge, we propose Quantile AlignTree Flow Matching (QAT-FM), an efficient structured coupling strategy that constructs a hierarchical coupling between a Gaussian prior and the target data distribution via a quantile-aligned tree structure. QAT-FM constructs the coupling in $\mathcal{O}(Nd\log N)$ time and supports per-pair source sampling with $\mathcal{O}(d)$ complexity, enabling scalable training for large-scale high-dimensional generative tasks. Theoretically, we prove that the QAT coupling satisfies marginal consistency, induces non-crossing linear interpolation paths, and consistently improves path separation at intermediate times compared with independent coupling, thereby alleviating local velocity ambiguity. QAT-FM further extends naturally to conditional generation, enabling structured conditional coupling while preserving global Gaussian alignment. Experiments across diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate that QAT-FM achieves competitive generative performance while substantially reducing coupling construction cost.

title: Large-Language Models as a Cognitive Virus
abstract: Large-language models (LLMs) are rapidly becoming part of human culture, reshaping how information is produced, transmitted, and used. Here we propose that their diffusion can be understood through a viral analogy, with LLM use spreading through populations, becoming embedded in cognitive and cultural practices. We model transitions among uncoupled, coupled, and persistently dependent users, and show that the interplay between social transmission, recovery, and collective reinforcement can generate tipping points and technological lock-in. A central consequence is the possibility of runaway dynamics: once a critical threshold is crossed, small increases in adoption can trigger rapid population-level shifts toward persistent dependence, with abrupt losses in cognitive competence. The same framework, however, identifies conditions for cognitive immunization, based on reducing transmission and facilitating reversibility. Our results highlight how LLM adoption may involve nonlinear collective transitions with important consequences for cognitive autonomy.

title: Desenrotllament d'un sistema de classificació de càncer de pell en imatges histològiques mitjançant models fundacionals i aprenentatge múltiple per instàncies
abstract: [ES] El análisis histológico constituye una herramienta clave en el diagnóstico de patologías oncológicas como el cáncer de piel, ya que permite evaluar con precisión el estado del tejido a nivel microscópico. En los últimos años, el uso de técnicas de inteligencia artificial ha supuesto un avance significativo en la automatización e interpretación de estas imágenes, posicionándose como una línea de investigación prometedora en patología digital. Las imágenes histológicas de alta resolución presentan un tamaño gigapíxel que imposibilita su procesamiento directo mediante redes convolucionales estándar. Por ello, los modelos de aprendizaje múltiple por instancias (Multiple Instance Learning, MIL) se han consolidado como el paradigma dominante para su análisis, permitiendo trabajar sobre regiones locales de la imagen sin necesidad de anotaciones a nivel de píxel. En este proyecto, se desarrolla un sistema basado en aprendizaje profundo para la clasificación automatizada de imágenes histológicas de cáncer de piel, empleando modelos fundacionales como extractores de características a nivel de parche. Sobre las representaciones obtenidas, se implementarán modelos MIL entrenados bajo diferentes paradigmas de aprendizaje, evaluando su capacidad predictiva e interpretabilidad como herramienta de apoyo al diagnóstico clínico.

title: Adaptive Geometry Topology for Quantum Simulation
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum simulation technique leveraging adaptive geometry topology. The core concept is to construct a quantum simulator by mapping the system's geometry to a dynamically evolving topology, allowing for enhanced representation of complex physical systems and improved prediction of stability. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through the simulation of a two-dimensional system, showcasing its ability to accurately capture intricate patterns and predict outcomes with significantly reduced computational cost compared to traditional methods. The method's advantages include enhanced representation of topological features, improved stability analysis, and potential for scaling to larger systems.

title: Self-Adaptive Graph Neural Networks for Automated Generation
abstract: The goal of this paper is to develop a novel approach to automated generation using self-adaptive graph neural networks (SA-GNNs). Traditional graph neural networks (GNNs) often struggle with adapting to dynamic data, limiting their effectiveness in complex generative tasks. This work introduces a new model, termed SA-GNN, that dynamically adjusts the network's structure and parameters based on input data, enabling the generation of higher-quality outputs. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through a series of experiments utilizing various generative datasets, showcasing superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. This paper presents a complete framework for automated generation, focusing on a robust and adaptable approach to represent and generate data.

title: 基于量子拓扑的计算资源分配优化
abstract: Quantum computing, leveraging the principles of quantum mechanics, holds immense promise for revolutionizing various fields, including drug discovery, materials science, and artificial intelligence. However, realizing this potential requires sophisticated and efficient resource allocation, a challenge currently addressed by traditional optimization methods. This paper introduces a novel framework, "Quantum Topology Allocation Optimization" (QTAO), designed to optimize the allocation of computational resources within quantum computing systems, specifically focusing on leveraging the unique properties of quantum spacetime. The core mechanism centers around the inherent structure of quantum systems – the topology – allowing for an optimization strategy that transcends conventional approaches. We demonstrate the effectiveness of QTAO through a series of simulations and analyses, showcasing improved resource utilization and enhanced quantum algorithm performance. This research represents a significant step forward in optimizing quantum computing infrastructure, paving the way for more reliable and efficient quantum computations.

title: Dynamic Probability Matrix Quantum Computing Applications
abstract: This paper investigates the application of dynamic probability matrices in quantum computing to enhance computational efficiency and precision. Traditional quantum algorithms often rely on complex probability matrices to represent and manipulate quantum states, presenting significant challenges in terms of computational cost and error mitigation. We propose a novel dynamic probability matrix design that leverages the inherent properties of quantum mechanics to optimize quantum computations. This design systematically adjusts the probability amplitudes to minimize error propagation and maximize the fidelity of quantum operations. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through a series of simulations and analyses, showcasing significant improvements in key performance metrics compared to existing quantum algorithms. The resulting dynamic probability matrix offers a promising avenue for accelerating quantum computing research and development.

title: Dynamic Topology-Dependent Quantum Error Correction Coding
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to quantum error correction (QEC) that dynamically adapts to topological disturbances encountered during quantum information transmission. The core concept revolves around leveraging machine learning to predict these disturbances and subsequently designing reconfigurable error-correcting codes. Traditional QEC methods often rely on static coding schemes, which are inherently vulnerable to the fluctuating topological environment. Our proposed framework utilizes a predictive model to anticipate the patterns of topological disruption, enabling the real-time adjustment of the coding structure. This dynamic adjustment is achieved by modifying the correlations between qubits, effectively mitigating the detrimental effects of the topological noise. The theoretical framework outlines a system where the error correction efficiency is maximized by responding to the specific characteristics of the quantum channel. The key contributions lie in the integration of machine learning for predictive modeling and the design of adaptable coding strategies, offering a significant advancement over conventional static QEC approaches. The ultimate goal is a more robust and efficient quantum communication system.

title: Quantum Memory Encoding for Neural Networks
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum memory encoding to revolutionize neural network design and performance. We propose a novel framework where neural network weights and activations are directly encoded into quantum states, exploiting quantum phenomena like superposition and entanglement to achieve enhanced computational capabilities. Specifically, we investigate methods for mapping classical neural network parameters to qubit states and introduce mechanisms for performing parallel computations. Our approach aims to dramatically increase the representational capacity of neural networks, potentially leading to accelerated learning rates and improved model accuracy. This work lays the groundwork for a fundamentally new approach to artificial intelligence, bridging the gap between classical and quantum computing. The core claim is that utilizing quantum memory encoding techniques within neural networks can significantly increase the representational capacity and accelerate learning. The core mechanism involves encoding neural network weights and activations into quantum states, leveraging superposition and entanglement to perform computations in parallel.

title: Graph-Based Anomaly Detection using Topological Diffusion
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to anomaly detection leveraging topological diffusion processes on graph representations of data. Traditional anomaly detection techniques often falter when dealing with intricate, high-dimensional datasets. Our method addresses this limitation by constructing a graph where data points are nodes and relationships between them are represented by edges. We then apply a diffusion process to this graph, iteratively propagating information across connected nodes. Anomalous data points, by their nature, disrupt this diffusion process, leading to measurable alterations in the graph's topology – specifically, changes in node degrees, clustering coefficients, and global network properties. These changes serve as indicators of anomalies. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through theoretical analysis and a conceptual framework, outlining the key parameters and considerations for implementation. The core claim of this work is that existing anomaly detection methods struggle with complex, high-dimensional data, and that topological diffusion offers a promising solution by providing a robust and interpretable method for detecting deviations from normal patterns. The method's reliance on graph structure makes it adaptable to various data types and provides insights into the underlying data relationships, beyond simply flagging outliers.

title: Algorithmic Chaos – A Self-Organizing Machine Learning Framework
abstract: This paper introduces an algorithmic chaos framework for machine learning, leveraging chaotic dynamics to enhance the training of neural networks. The core mechanism centers around a feedback loop inspired by fractal geometry, dynamically shaping the network's output through a simulated chaotic system. This approach aims to promote robustness and generalization, moving beyond traditional supervised learning techniques. We detail the framework's architecture, explain the chaotic system's role, and analyze its potential benefits.

title: Probabilistic Programming for Robotic Reinforcement Learning
abstract: This paper explores the application of probabilistic programming languages (PPLs) to robotic reinforcement learning (RL). Traditional RL methods often struggle with uncertainty and require extensive hand-tuning to perform reliably in real-world environments. This work argues that PPLs offer a significant advantage by allowing the direct representation and reasoning about uncertainty within the RL framework. Specifically, we propose leveraging PPLs to model the robot's environment, actions, and rewards, thereby facilitating the implementation of Bayesian RL algorithms. This approach simplifies system design and enhances adaptability by allowing the algorithm to learn from noisy data and incorporate prior knowledge. The core claim is that PPLs will lead to more robust and adaptable RL systems for robots. We present a framework for utilizing PPLs in this context, focusing on the key elements of environmental modeling, action and reward modeling, and the integration with Bayesian RL techniques. The primary benefit is a reduced need for manual hyperparameter tuning and increased resilience to unforeseen environmental variations. This work highlights the potential of PPLs as a foundational technology for advancing the field of robotic RL.

title: 基于图的自适应矩阵学习
abstract: This paper introduces a novel method for matrix learning based on graph-structured representations. Traditional approaches often rely on gradient descent, which can be computationally expensive and may struggle with complex data. Our method leverages graph structures to dynamically control the learning process, resulting in improved accuracy and efficiency. We propose a framework where the matrix is represented as a graph, and the learning algorithm adjusts the graph structure to optimize the matrix's representation. This adaptive approach allows for more efficient learning and potentially better generalization performance. We present the theoretical foundations of the proposed method, demonstrate its effectiveness through various numerical experiments, and discuss its advantages and limitations. The core mechanism focuses on leveraging graph properties to guide the matrix update process.
